25: # Tone of Voice
26: 
27: Produce a `TONE.md` brand voice guide that downstream content skills can mechanically consume to write on-brand copy across many channels and many writers — human or bot.
28: 
29: ## Why this skill exists
30: 
31: Most tone-of-voice work ends up as a PDF nobody reads. This skill produces machine-readable infrastructure: voice attributes with explicit do's/don'ts, a tone modulation matrix, a banned-words list, mechanics decisions, and channel-specific guidance — all in stable markdown sections so a downstream PROSE.md generator (or any writing skill or bot) can parse and apply it.
32: 
33: **Voice vs tone is load-bearing.** Voice is the fixed personality of the brand (does not change). Tone is the contextual modulation across channel, audience, situation. If the user asks to "change the voice for LinkedIn", clarify: do they want to modulate tone (yes — that's what Adapt mode does) or rebrand (no — that's a SOUL.md change). Confusing the two is the single most common failure mode in this work.
34: 
35: ## When to invoke
36: 
37: Invoke when the user wants to:
38: 
39: - Create a brand TONE.md / tone-of-voice guide
40: - Adapt an existing TONE.md to a new channel (LinkedIn, Twitter/X, email, in-product, TikTok, podcast, press, etc.)
41: - Define voice attributes, lexicon, and channel rules for a content factory
42: - Refresh an outdated voice
43: 
44: Skip when:
45: 
46: - The user wants a brand identity / mission / values document → `SOUL.md` (separate skill)
47: - The user wants prose-style conventions for code or docs → `PROSE.md` (separate skill, consumes TONE.md)
48: - The user wants visual design rules (colours, typography, spacing) → `DESIGN.md` (separate skill)
49: - The user is asking about a specific piece of content, not the system
50: 
51: ## Inputs
52: 
53: - **Optional**: `SOUL.md` in the working directory (or a path the user supplies). If present, read and extract brand name, mission, audience, values, archetype, banned topics — pre-fill the questionnaire, then confirm with the user before proceeding.
54: - **Required**: user answers to the discovery questions (Phase 1).
55: - **Adapt mode**: path to the existing `TONE.md` plus the target channel.
56: 
57: ## Output
58: 
59: - **`TONE.md`** at the working directory root (or the path the user supplies). Structure defined in [assets/TONE-template.md](assets/TONE-template.md).
60: - **Adapt mode**: either appends a channel section to the existing TONE.md or writes `TONE-<channel>.md`. Ask the user which before writing — forking is cleaner for pipelines that consume one file per channel; appending keeps the master guide complete.
61: 
62: ---
63: 
64: ## Create mode
65: 
66: ### Phase 1 — Discovery (interview)
67: 
68: Skim [references/discovery-questionnaire.md](references/discovery-questionnaire.md) — it contains the exhaustive 80+ question bank. The batches below are the **minimum** to produce a usable TONE.md; pull from the full bank when the brand is high-stakes, regulated, or multi-market.
69: 
70: 1. **Glob for `SOUL.md`** in CWD. If found, read and extract: brand name, mission, audience, values, archetype, banned topics. Display the extraction and ask the user to confirm or correct. Skip the questions that SOUL.md already answers.
71: 
72: 2. **Batch A — basics** (single `AskUserQuestion` call, 4 questions):
73:    - Mode: Create from scratch / Adapt existing TONE.md
74:    - Brand category: B2B SaaS, B2C/D2C, NGO, Public Sector, Consulting, Industrial, Personal brand, Volunteering, Political/Advocacy, Other
75:    - Primary market(s) and language(s) — country and locale matter for idiom, reading age, and humour calibration
76:    - Primary content goal: Demand gen, Awareness, Retention, Recruiting, Fundraising, Advocacy, Internal comms, Other
77: 
78: 3. **Batch B — audience & channels** (4 questions):
79:    - Primary audience (single persona, free text — multi-persona handled in follow-up)
80:    - Channels in scope (multi-select): Web, Blog, Email, LinkedIn, Twitter/X, TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, Podcast, In-product UI, Support, Press, Sales decks, Recruiting, Other
81:    - Reading-age target: Adult general / Expert+technical / Reading-age 9 (gov + inclusive default) / Mixed
82:    - Risk tolerance: Safe & neutral / Moderately distinctive / Boldly distinctive (willing to alienate non-buyers)
83: 
84: 4. **Batch C — personality & references** (4 questions):
85:    - Primary archetype guess: 12 Jung options (Innocent, Sage, Explorer, Outlaw, Magician, Hero, Lover, Jester, Everyman, Caregiver, Ruler, Creator) or Unsure
86:    - Voice references: 3-5 admired brands to triangulate from (free text)
87:    - Anti-references: 3-5 brands NOT to sound like (free text)
88:    - Founder/CEO voice contribution: Heavy / Moderate / None / Explicitly avoid
89: 
90: 5. **Batch D — constraints** (3-4 questions):
91:    - Regulatory regime: None / GDPR / HIPAA / FDA / SEC / FCA / ASA / Other
92:    - Cultural taboos and topics to avoid (free text)
93:    - Existing brand book / banned-word list (path or None)
94:    - Localisation strategy: Single locale / Multi-locale with shared voice / Per-locale voice
95: 
96: If the user's category is "Other" or sits outside the covered set in [references/category-adaptations.md](references/category-adaptations.md) — politics, religious organisations, defense, gaming, healthcare professional comms, adult content, sports teams, fintech-crypto — proceed to Phase 2.
97: 
98: ### Phase 2 — Research uncovered contexts (conditional)
99: 
100: Spawn an Agent sub-task with this brief:
101: 
102: > Research current tone-of-voice norms for `<category>` brands in `<market>`. Cover: 1) typical voice attributes for the category; 2) common pitfalls and how audiences react to off-tone copy; 3) 2-3 reference brands with publicly observable voice patterns (cite primary sources); 4) regulatory, cultural, or platform constraints on voice. Report in under 700 words with sources cited inline.
103: 
104: For broad cross-market research (e.g. political comms across regions), spawn up to 3 parallel agents split by region or sub-category, then synthesise the findings before continuing to Phase 3.
105: 
106: Use the agent's output to populate the category-adaptation section of TONE.md and refine voice attributes. Footnote sources — future maintainers will need to verify when category norms shift.
107: 
108: ### Phase 3 — Define voice (ultrathink)
109: 
110: Use `ultrathink` for this phase. Synthesise the discovery inputs into:
111: 
112: 1. **NN/g 4 dimensions position** — funny/serious, formal/casual, respectful/irreverent, enthusiastic/matter-of-fact. Each is a 3-point scale. Do **not** cluster all four near midpoint — defaulting to mid-range scores produces bland, forgettable voices that fail to differentiate from category default. Lean to one side on at least three of the four dimensions.
113: 
114: 2. **3-5 voice attributes**, each in the "X but never Y" pattern (Slack: "Confident, never cocky; Witty, but never silly"). For each, produce: one-line definition, 3 do's, 3 don'ts, 1 example sentence, 1 anti-example pulled from the brand's own past content if possible. Three is the minimum (fewer is unhelpful); five is the maximum (more is unmemorable). See [references/voice-attributes.md](references/voice-attributes.md) for the documentation pattern.
115: 
116: 3. **Primary archetype** (optional secondary). Don't over-commit to archetype — it is a positioning shortcut, not a voice solution. Brands that lean too hard on archetype end up in cosplay (every "Hero" brand sounds the same).
117: 
118: 4. **Tone modulation matrix** — rows are situations (launch, crisis, complaint, win, sensitive topic, routine, sales objection, layoffs/bad news, apology), columns are the channels in scope. Each cell: dominant tone + 2-3 prohibited tones. This is the operational core — downstream writers and bots consult this more than the principles narrative.
119: 
120: 5. **Lexicon** — preferred terms (named concepts, customer noun like "members" vs "users"), banned terms (jargon, marketing clichés, exclusionary language), power words (10-30), jargon policy (when allowed for which audience), naming conventions (brand, product, features, competitors). See [references/lexicon-mechanics.md](references/lexicon-mechanics.md).
121: 
122: 6. **Mechanics** — person (1st plural "we" / 2nd "you"), contractions (yes/no/contextual; GOV.UK avoids negative contractions because they harm non-native readers), Oxford comma, sentence length norm (general public: average 15-20 words; expert audiences may go longer), active/passive default (active unless softening a sensitive message), sentence case vs title case, emoji policy, punctuation tics (ellipses, em-dashes, exclamation marks), numerals. Same reference file.
123: 
124: 7. **Inclusive language** — base on the Conscious Style Guide (Karen Yin) and APA Inclusive Language Guidelines. Decide gendered language policy, ability/disability terms, race, age, nationality, neurodiversity. Per market if multi-locale.
125: 
126: 8. **Channel-specific guidance** — apply [references/channel-adaptations.md](references/channel-adaptations.md) per channel in scope, capturing hard platform constraints (character limits, format) and tonal shifts.
127: 
128: ### Phase 4 — Write TONE.md
129: 
130: Use [assets/TONE-template.md](assets/TONE-template.md). Fill every section. **Section names and structure are stable** — downstream skills depend on them for parsing.
131: 
132: Mandatory sections (order matters for downstream pipelines):
133: 
134: - Context (brand, market, channels, goal)
135: - Voice attributes (3-5, each with do/don't/example/anti-example)
136: - Archetype
137: - NN/g 4 dimensions positioning
138: - Tone modulation matrix
139: - Lexicon (preferred, banned, power words)
140: - Mechanics
141: - Inclusive language
142: - Channel-specific guidance (one subsection per channel in scope)
143: - **Global Do's and Don'ts** (consolidated, scannable list — this is what writers paste into their context window when drafting)
144: - Examples library (before/after pairs)
145: 
146: ### Phase 5 — Validate
147: 
148: Run these checks before finalising the file. If any fails, surface the gap and ask the user before writing the final TONE.md:
149: 
150: - 3-5 voice attributes — neither fewer nor more.
151: - Every attribute has at least one anti-example sourced from the brand's own context (not a generic placeholder like "lorem ipsum bad").
152: - NN/g positions don't all cluster near midpoint — at least 3 of 4 dimensions clearly off-centre.
153: - Banned-words list is non-empty (prevention is cheaper than prescription — without it, writers default to category clichés the brand wanted to avoid).
154: - One channel-specific subsection per channel in scope.
155: - Sample three random do's and three random don'ts and re-read: would a new writer or bot know exactly what to do tomorrow? If they're abstract, rewrite them as concrete sentences with examples.
156: 
157: ---
158: 
159: ## Adapt mode
160: 
161: For porting an existing TONE.md to a new support or channel without rebuilding the whole guide.
162: 
163: 1. Read the existing `TONE.md`. Confirm with the user that **voice attributes do not change** — only tone modulates per channel. If the user disagrees, redirect them to SOUL.md (rebrand) or to Create mode (new TONE.md).
164: 2. Ask target channel via `AskUserQuestion`: LinkedIn / Twitter-X / Email / In-product UI / Podcast / Video script / Press release / TikTok / Instagram / YouTube / Sales deck / Other.
165: 3. Ask whether to **append** a channel section to the existing TONE.md or **fork** a new `TONE-<channel>.md`. Forking is cleaner for content-factory pipelines that load one file per channel; appending keeps the master guide complete.
166: 4. Apply the relevant section of [references/channel-adaptations.md](references/channel-adaptations.md) — each channel documents hard constraints (character limits, format, supported markdown), tonal shifts (e.g. LinkedIn dampens irreverence; TikTok rewards cadence and trend-awareness; in-product UI strips flourish), and prohibited registers.
167: 5. Re-derive 3 do's and 3 don'ts specific to the channel. Pull from the global list but make them concrete to the medium (a do that reads "be concise" globally becomes "lead with the verb in the first 90 characters" for Twitter/X).
168: 6. Re-do the relevant column of the tone modulation matrix.
169: 7. Write the adapted section or new file.
170: 
171: ---
172: 
173: ## Important constraints
174: 
175: - **Voice does not change. Tone does.** If you find yourself rewriting voice attributes for a channel, stop — that's a SOUL.md change, not a channel adaptation.
176: - **No PDF outputs, no decorative formatting.** TONE.md is plain markdown so any downstream skill or bot can parse it deterministically. Avoid ASCII art, complex tables in voice-attribute sections, or anything that breaks markdown parsers.
177: - **Cite sources for research-derived claims.** When Phase 2 research informs the TONE.md, footnote the source in the category section — future maintainers will need to verify when norms shift (especially fast-moving categories like gaming and crypto).
178: - **Don't borrow voices wholesale.** "We want to sound like Oatly / Mailchimp / Duolingo" briefs produce derivative voices that audiences increasingly detect (especially when AI-written). Use references to triangulate, not imitate. The strategy under the style is what makes a voice work, not the surface mannerisms.
179: - **Banned-words lists do more work than power-words lists.** Prevention is cheaper than prescription — a writer encountering "we don't use 'leverage' (unless in the financial sense)" never reaches for it again. A power-words list, by contrast, is rarely consulted in the moment.
180: - **Politics, regulated industries, religious organisations, defense, healthcare professional comms, gaming, adult content, sports teams, fintech-crypto** → research first via Phase 2. Do not apply consumer-brand defaults. Each has voice norms shaped by audience, regulation, and platform that override generic guidance.
181: - **For multi-locale brands**, document voice per locale rather than translating from one source language. Transcreation is the standard; surface-translating English brand voice into French or Japanese produces tin-eared copy that fails the local market.
182: 
183: ## Disclaimer
184: 
185: This skill is not exhaustive. The discipline of tone of voice is evolving rapidly, especially as AI-generated content shifts where differentiation lives. Refer to canonical sources for current best practice: Mailchimp's content style guide, GOV.UK's style guide, Nielsen Norman Group's _The Four Dimensions of Tone of Voice_, Karen Yin's Conscious Style Guide, Margot Bloomstein's _Trustworthy_, and the published voice guides of the brands in [references/reference-brands.md](references/reference-brands.md). Voice norms vary by category and locale; verify any pattern that surprises you against the brand's actual category and market before committing it to TONE.md.
186:

191: - [references/voice-attributes.md](references/voice-attributes.md) — attribute documentation pattern, NN/g 4 dimensions, Jung archetypes

It's a big model (2.8T parameters) and quite token-inefficient. It is half as expensive as GPT-5.6-Sol on a per-token basis but uses twice as many tokens as Sol, balancing out the costs.

But it doesn't have vision, i.e. you can't attach images in your prompts. This post covers how to add vision capabilities to GLM-5.2 without sacrificing intelligence.

Labs would share models up to 30 days early for cybersecurity, biological risk and deception tests - voluntarily at first, with deployment approval possible later.

241: and there's a new sonnet
242:

244: 
245:  Fable is back
246:  and there's a new sonnet
247:  Jul 2
248: 
249:  READ IN APP
250: 
251:  Hey folks,
252: 
253:  When I was in Greece, I needed to organise a taxi from the airport home. I pinged codex and 1m37s later it was done, I got a text to say the car was booked.
254:  Codex also added the redacted bit to this image
255: 
256:  It's not the most impressive task by all means but there's a system as to why it works (and this system is how a lot of tasks work).
257: 
258:  So first, all my day-to-day agent conversations start in my 'bites' folder, which has links to files that store my memories, what I'm working on, ben's bites, about me etc.
259: 
260:  Codex loads my AGENTS.md and my task then gets to work.
261: 
262:  It's got the default Google Calendar and Gmail tools connected, so starts with looking at if my flight is in my calendar (which it was, thanks to another Codex thread I did pre-trip). Finds the trip and then looks in my emails for any prior task/transfer emails, finds one to get my home address and the company I used on the way out (these could also be noted in my folders' files, in a 'TRAVEL.md' file, linked from my AGENTS.md).
263: 
264:  So now it's got all the details it needs, this is the 'agenty' bit, it's gathered enough context to complete my task. With that context it determines the next thing to do: make the booking. It knows the tools it has available to it, like computer use, so it went on to the taxi's website (I had my computer stay on all trip so I could connect), filled in the booking form and made the payment.
265: 
266:  Working with agents is a lot about making sure the right context and tools are available to do the task. If both are covered, agents can get stuff done without you interfering.
267: 
268:  We have to think about tasks in this way - what would an agent (or a person) need if they had no knowledge of you or your task? It's your job to make sure it's available.
269: 
270:  Let's get to it.
271: 
272:  p.s. I wanted to shout out my friend's first business he launched solo - Fixxa - voice quotes and invoices for UK tradespeople, with WhatsApp delivery and Stripe links.
273: 
274:  Ben's Bites is brought to you by Attio

Fable 5 is only included in the subscription plans till July 7 and you can only use 50% of your limits on Fable. This benchmark claims Fable can do 16% of remote work projects, double the amount of Opus 4.8.

It is now the default for Free/Pro, available in Claude Code and API, and has launch pricing of $2/$10 per million tokens until Aug 31. 316: 
317:  Hey folks, I'm back from a long weekend in Greece and have to tell you about a company I backed a couple years ago that's coming out of stealth.
318: 
319:  Etched.
320: 
321:  Training got all the attention for the last few years. But in 2026, the real fight is serving intelligence: lower latency, lower cost, less power, more tokens. The market is screaming for better inference systems, and we've never seen a market like inference. So much so, people can't sleep thinking about it (see the tweet in afters 😂).
322: 
323:  AI inference could be the biggest market in history and the bottleneck is inference hardware. Etched built the perfect product. Pulling it off will change how models run.
324: 
325:  Etched are building frontier inference clusters with extreme vertical integration: chips, racks, software, manufacturing, and production co-designed end to end. First product in under three years, while most hardware peers took 7+.
326: 
327:  Their traction is already insane: $800M raised, $1B+ in backlog orders, production underway with TSMC, and first chips working on the very first try (A0) on TSMC 4nm. A0 means the first physical version of a chip/system design that comes back from the fab. So yeah, A0 success is hard. Doing it this fast is wild.
328: 
329:  I backed Gavin in 2023, as a 21-year old Harvard dropout, because he had first-principles technical conviction and the ability to recruit the most insane team who had actually built the last generation of compute infrastructure. Now Etched is 400+ people from NVIDIA, Google TPU, Broadcom, SK Hynix, TSMC and basically every serious AI chip program.
330: 
331:  They're backed by VentureTech Alliance (which has a strong partnership w/ TSMC), Peter Thiel, Jane Street, Two Sigma, Jump, HRT, Stripes, Ribbit and more.
332: 
333:  As we're seeing, who wins in AI won't just be decided by who has the best models. But by who can serve them.
334: 
335:  Ben's Bites is brought to you by Render
336: 
337:  Chainable compute. Right on queue.
338: 
339:  Define tasks with Render's lightweight SDK and chain them into long-running, distributed workflows. Launch your agents and batch jobs on demand. Render Workflows handles queuing, orchestration, and retries.

Sol is the biggest/smartest one of the bunch. It bypasses Mythos in certain benchmarks but is conveniently a little shy of Mythos-level in exploiting cybersecurity bugs. Sam Altman claims that GPT-5.6 will be available to regular users soon—though it might be US only to begin with, even if he's working hard for worldwide.

372: Name: AI with Remy
373: Subject: the simplest team second brain setup
374: Body:
375: plus, Kimi K3 is near-fable intelligence at sonnet prices
376: 
377: Read online
378: 
379:  I've got something exciting to share…
380: 
381:  I put together a perks page for you as a thank you for being subscribed :)
382: 
383:  $5k+ of discounts on the software you're probably already paying for: Notion, Cursor, ElevenLabs, OpenRouter, Granola, and about 300 more.
384: 
385:  check them out at aiwithremy.com/deals
386: 
387:  If you're paying for even two or three tools on that page, this is the most valuable link in today's issue.
388: 
389:  📌 TL;DR
390: 
391:   * Kimi K3 is here → the first open model I'd actually use. #1 in the world for frontend, near-Fable smarts at Sonnet prices.
392:   * Claude Code artifacts go live → the web pages Claude builds can now pull your real data every time they load. Build your team a live dashboard - ad performance, cash flow, whatever - straight from a chat.
393:   * Builder's notes → I gave claude access to my 1password, and why I ditched obsidian
394: 
395:  Kimi K3: we finally have a Chinese Anthropic
396: 
397:  I have never been a fan of open-source models so far. They are cheaper, sure, but never on the level of Claude or the OpenAI models.
398: 
399:  Kimi K3 (from Moonshot AI) is the first one I'd genuinely use.
400: 
401:  Tweet screenshot
402: 
403:  It's exceptional at coding, and especially at front-end design - the actual look and feel of apps and websites - where it seams to beat Claude Fable 5 and GPT 5.6 Sol.
404: 
405:  here are some highlights…
406: 
407:  Tweet screenshot
408: 
409:  Tweet screenshot
410: 
411:  K3 took #1 on the Frontend Code Arena (the leaderboard for building the actual UI of apps and sites) - a 17-place jump from Kimi's last model, topping 6 of 7 categories.
412: 
413:  Overall it's more measured: 3rd on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index (a broad "how smart across everything" score), level with Opus 4.8, behind Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol.
414: 
415:  k3 lands third on the intelligence index: level with opus 4.8, behind only fable 5 and gpt-5.6 sol
416: 
417:  And then you look at the price. K3 runs $3 in / $15 out per million tokens. That's Sonnet-level pricing for near-Fable intelligence, about half the cost of Opus per task.
418: 
419:  They claim it's just as strong at knowledge work too, but I haven't tested it, so don't take my word for it there.
420: 
421:  But for coding and especially web/ app design work… K3 is the one for you to be using.
422: 
423:  How to start using it:
424: 
425:  Skip Kimi's own apps, grab the $40/month Kimi subscription, and run the model inside the tools you already use…
426: 
427:   * OpenCode (a free, open-source Claude Code clone) with your API key.
428:   * Or Claude Code itself via a CLI proxy (a small bit of software that reroutes it to Kimi).
429:   * Use the OpenRouter MCP to get claude to delegate tasks to K3
430: 
431:  Two caveats: it's 2-3x slower than Claude, and until the weights land on July 27 everything routes through Chinese servers.
432: 
433:  Claude Code can now build you a live dashboard from a chat
434: 
435:  Artifacts are the live web pages Claude Code can publish straight out of a session to a private claude.ai URL. you ask it to build a little tool or page, and it hands you back a real link.
436: 
437:  Share session output as artifacts
438: 
439:  Well those pages can now call your connectors every time someone opens them (connectors = the links between Claude and your actual tools - Notion, Stripe, Linear, Google, that lot).
440: 
441:  So instead of a snapshot frozen at the moment it was built, the page pulls current data every time it loads. And it can take actions too - post a message, update an issue.
442: 
443:  This is a great way to build proper web apps for you and your team…
444: 
445:  Think an ad-performance dashboard, a finance tracker, a cash-flow projector. All wired into live data from the tools you already use, built in a chat, no code.
446: 
447:  A few things to get right:
448: 
449:   * You need a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan and Claude Code v2.1.209+.
450:   * An artifact with connectors in it, can never be shared to a public link, on any plan. Team and Enterprise can share it inside the org.
451:   * Local MCP servers don't work in the published page (those are connectors running on your own computer). Only claude.ai account connectors do.
452: 
453:  Full write-up is in Anthropic's announcement.
454: 
455:  Also this week...
456: 
457:   * Notion now opens Markdown files → it's an "Open with" shortcut on desktop, that opens your markdown file into notion, alongside an “import to notion” option
458: 
459:   * Fable 5 is coming back to your plan → from July 20 it's included in all Max and Team Premium plans (at 50% of limits), and Pro / Team Standard users get a one-time $100 credit instead. A nice sequel to Fable “leaving” your plan on the 12th.
460: 
461:  💡 Builder's notes
462: 
463:  1Password is now my API key manager - and Claude can use it too.
464: 
465:  1Password is a password manager (it keeps all your logins and secrets behind one master password). What I've been doing this week is wiring it into my agents.
466: 
467:  It has a CLI - a command-line version of the app - and that lets an agent like Claude Code pull secrets straight from your vault.
468: 
469:  Sounds terrifying, I know. But here's the bit that makes it safe: every single time Claude tries to grab something, a pop-up appears on your screen. You approve it with Touch ID or your password, and only then does Claude get that one thing.
470: 
471:  It doesn't have blanket access to everything.
472: 
473:  So now, instead of keeping my API keys in ENV files (plain text files where devs usually stash their keys, sitting unencrypted on your machine), they all live in 1Password.
474: 
475:  Same trick's been handy with the team. Instead of pasting a login into Slack, I share it as a 1Password link that expires after 3 days.
476: 
477:  Create expiring links for secure sharing, and share items and passwords with anyone, even if they don't have 1Password.
478: 
479:  The simplest & most effective version of a company second brain…
480: 
481:  I've moved off Obsidian for a little while now, for two reasons.
482: 
483:   * Obsidian is built to be a personal second brain - you're dumping in sources from all over the internet, meeting notes, and more. That's not something you want synced to your whole company.
484: 
485:   * It all lives locally on your computer. So the moment you set up agents in the cloud, they can't reach any of it.
486: 
487:  I've since set up Garry Tan's gbrain and it's been working well.
488: 
489:  But that's not actually my recommendation for most people.
490: 
491:  The simplest company brain i...

501: 
502:  Good evening folks,
503: 
504:  The AI course: six live sessions over two weeks, sold out on Tuesday 🍾
505: 
506:  I havent been so excited for a project in a while!
507: 
508:  📌 TL;DR
509: 
510:   * GPT-5.6 → OpenAI's new family (Sol, Terra, Luna) is out, and Every ran it for a month before anyone else. Their verdict: a Porsche to Fable's warp drive, a much better writer, and the first model that can run whole loops of work on its own.
511: 
512:   * Claude Cowork runs with your laptop shut → hand it a task at your desk, pick up the finished work on your phone. Scheduled jobs now run with no device online at all. Beta, Max plan first.
513: 
514:   * Notion's Agent Hub → run your custom Notion agents from your phone. Native to your workspace and multiplayer, so the whole team shares one agent. Firmly the automation side, not the cockpit.
515: 
516:   * Grok 4.5 → cheap, fast, "a weirdly good default code model" at $2 / $6. Free for a limited time in Cursor and Grok Build. Proof that models matter less and less now.
517: 
518:   * Builder's notes → I built Ledger, my own finance app, and folded every subscription into it. Plus 3 prompts to run before Fable 5 leaves your plan on July 12.
519: 
520:  GPT-5.6: the model Every has been secretly running for a month
521: 
522:  OpenAI shipped GPT-5.6 today, but the story worth reading isn't the launch post. It's that Dan Shipper and his team at Every had it for about a month before the rest of us. They were one of ~20 early partners running it, and their verdict just dropped.
523: 
524:  So I'll let them carry this one.
525:

829:  A few pieces still needed their final touches: the onboarding flow when you join the program, locking in session times, and finishing the last bits of the curriculum, so it's the most valuable (and digestible) it can be whether you're a total beginner or already running these agents every day.
830: 
831:  So pumped to release this in a week's time and get you MFs AI power users!
832: 
833:  Here's the waitlist link in case you missed it: aiwithremy.com/waitlist (only 60 spots, and 890 of you on the list now), and waitlisters get the early-bird discount.
834: 
835:  Cannes Lions oui oui
836: 
837:  📌 TL;DR
838: 
839:   * Sakana Fugu → Japan's "new model" is actually a router that auto-picks the best AI for each task. clever idea, but it's slow right now and didn't beat just using one good model. (no Fable 5 in its pool, and it doesn't care.)
840:   * Claude Tag → Anthropic dropped Claude into Slack as a teammate you @mention. it remembers context, takes real actions, and in ambient mode acts on its own. Team/Enterprise only, but the pattern's worth stealing.
841:   * Perplexity Brain → a real memory for your AI agent. it remembers the WORK, not just your preferences, and rewrites its own playbook overnight.
842:   * Builder's notes → the /teach skill that turns any folder into a tutor, how I finally nailed local vs cloud scheduled tasks, and Helm, a little VS Code extension I vibe-coded.
843: 
844:  Sakana Fugu, the AI that picks your AI for you
845: 
846:  Japan's Sakana AI dropped Fugu this week, and the internet instantly branded it a "Fable 5 killer."
847: 
848:  It's not. and don't let the hype fool you, Fugu isn't a new frontier model at all.
849: 
850:  It's a router (basically a smart switchboard). you hand it a task, and instead of you guessing "hmm which AI should I use for this?", it auto-picks the best model for the job, Opus, GPT-5.5 or Gemini, then fuses their answers back into one.
851: 
852:  Under the hood it's a small trained "conductor" that calls other labs' top models behind a single API. nothing to download, it's hosted only.
853: 
854:  Clever idea. not a brand new one, mind you, Perplexity's agent ("Computer", the thing that goes off and does tasks for you) already routes like this. but it's a cool concept.
855: 
856:  In real testing though, the cracks show…
857: 
858:  Jack Roberts (big name in the AI space) put Fugu up against Opus 4.8 and GLM 5.2. about 3.5x slower than Opus on a website build, and 3x as many tokens, because all that routing and stitching adds up. and it never clearly beat just using one good model on its own.
859: 
860:  GLM 5.2 was the standout for value. nobody dethroned Opus.
861: 
862:  Pricing's $20 / $100 / $200 a month (every tier includes both Fugu and Fugu Ultra), or pay-as-you-go Fugu Ultra at $5 in / $30 out per million tokens. no free tier, and it's not in the EU at launch.
863: 
864:  Bottom line, it's more tokens and slower answers today. but it'll get better, and the idea is the interesting part here, not the performance.
865: 
866:  not yet, anyway.
867: 
868:  Anthropic just put Claude inside Slack as an actual teammate
869: 
870:  This is one of the most exciting things Anthropic has shipped in a while.
871: 
872:  It's called Claude Tag, and it drops Claude straight into Slack as a teammate you @mention. it remembers context across days, takes real actions through your connected tools, and in "ambient mode" it can even act on its own.
873: 
874:  Here's how it works.
875: 
876:  You @mention @Claude in a channel or thread, it breaks your task into stages, works through them using whatever tools & skills it's hooked up to, then replies right there in the thread with what it made.
877: 
878:  Claude Tag: a scheduled weekly pipeline digest, posted on its own (ambient/scheduled task)
879: 
880:  The big shift is that it's multiplayer. one shared Claude per channel, so the whole team can see what it's doing and pick up where someone left off (a proper step up from the old 1:1 "Claude in Slack").
881: 
882:  it also builds context over time so nobody has to re-explain themselves, and with permission it can even learn from other channels.
883: 
884:  Ambient mode is defs the standout - this is where Claude stops waiting to be asked and takes initiative, flagging what it reckons you need, chasing loose ends, tagging the right people on its own.
885: 
886:  The example Anthropic gave: it spots a "can't log in" email from a customer and alerts both the support and engineering channels itself, before anyone's even noticed.
887: 
888:  Claude Tag: pulled and ranked account spend from BigQuery and charted it, in-thread
889: 
890:  For the bigger teams worried about it going haywire, there's proper control. admins decide which tools, channels and repos each "Claude identity" can touch, set spending caps (per org, per channel, per person), and manage skills centrally.
891: 
892:  Memory is walled off per channel, so sales never bleeds into engineering, and none of your conversations are used to train the models.
893: 
894:  It plugs into Gmail, HubSpot, Airtable, GitHub, Drive and all the usual apps you connect to your normal claude.
895: 
896:  Claude Tag: meeting prep pulled from calendar + CRM
897: 
898:  Now the but. it's Team and Enterprise only, it runs on Opus 4.8, and it replaces the old Claude Slack app completely.
899: 
900:  I can see this being really valuable for even a team of 1-5.
901: 
902:  they can spin up separate Slack channels for different parts of the business, marketing, finance, content, and run an always-on assistant in each, especially with ambient mode and scheduled check-ins.
903: 
904:  And you can just chat to @claude in a private slack dm if its just you, but you get to benefit from those more openclaw/ hermes style features.
905: 
906:  Anthropic says about 65% of its own product team's code now comes from their internal version of this.
907: 
908:  get started here

911:

953:  The Prompt That Writes Your Questions for the Doctor
954: 
955:  You've waited weeks to get the appointment. Now you're 15 minutes from the door.
956: 
957:  You already know not to ask AI what's wrong with you. Wrong diagnosis, wrong prognosis & you carry it into the room with you.
958: 
959:  So don't. Give it the mess and let it find the questions you'd forget to ask. I'm preparing for a medical appointment, either mine or one I'm taking someone to. Do not diagnose, and do not guess at what's wrong. Here's what's going on: [symptoms, how long, what's been tried, any test results] Organize it into: 1. A short timeline, in order. If this is a follow-up, focus on what's changed since the last visit. 2. Context worth mentioning: medications, family history, recent changes 3. Questions to ask, most important first 4. What to bring: records, test results, a list of medications 5. Signs that would mean not waiting for this appointment For 5, give me specific changes to watch for, not possible conditions. If what I've described already sounds like it needs care now, say that first.
960: 
961:  Why it works: You can describe what's happening to you. Turning that into the right questions is the hard part. It builds the list you'd only think of on the drive home. Item 5 does the other job. It tells you when not to wait for the appointment at all.
962: 
963:  One thing: It writes you 12 questions. You'll get through 3.
964: 
965:  Simple fix: Tell it how long the appointment is and ask it to cut the list to fit. ❝
966: 
967:  Advice spreads because the people it worked for repeat it.

971:  Add Up the Hidden Costs Before You Move or Switch
972: 
973:  The new place has an extra room and costs $50 less. You ran the numbers twice on your phone.
974: 
975:  Both times you left out first and last, the deposit, the truck, and the fee the internet company charges just to show up.
976: 
977:  Those wipe out a year of the savings.
978: 
979:  Swap in a job offer, a phone plan, or switching insurance. Anything where the price you see leaves things out.
980: 
981:  Turn on web search before you run this. It needs to look up what these things cost where you live. I'm deciding whether to switch or stay put, and I want the costs I'm not thinking about. Where I am: [city, or zip code] Staying: [what you pay now, what you get] Switching: [what you'd pay, what you'd get] Search the web for current costs in my area before you answer. Local fees are the point, don't estimate them from memory. 1. Find the one-time costs of switching that people forget, for my location. Deposits, utility activation, internet or cable install, building or HOA fees, agent and broker fees. 2. Ask what I'm avoiding by switching. Some costs disappear, like an agent fee I don't have to pay, and those count against the total. 3. List the ongoing costs that change, including ones that never show up on a bill. If my commute changes, ask for the distance and look up current fuel prices near me to price it. If I'm moving somewhere smaller, ask what won't fit and price storage. 4. Ask how long I plan to stay. If I don't know, use 2 years. Then give me: - The real first-year cost of each, one-time costs and savings included - Break-even: how long the monthly difference takes to cover the one-time costs - What I gain or give up that isn't money, and what that's worth against the number Use my numbers where I gave them, searched numbers where you found them, and label anything you estimated. Show your math.
982: 
983:  Why it works: It asks where you live, then looks up real fees instead of guessing at them. It also counts what you save. Not paying an agent can be worth a month's rent, and a side-by-side of the 2 rents never shows that.
984: 
985:  One thing: A fee it finds online might be for the wrong city.
986: 
987:  Simple fix: Ask it to name the city and the source for each number it looked up. 200+ Proven Ways to Make Money With AI in 2026

999:  The Prompt That Gets a 2nd Opinion on Any Advice
1000: 
1001:  Someone just told you what to do. A contractor, a video, a guy in a forum, the AI you asked.
1002: 
1003:  It sounded right. It usually does.
1004: 
1005:  Before you act, make it hold up against someone who would actually know. I'm about to act on this recommendation: [paste it] It came from: [a person, a video, an AI, a company selling something] My situation: [1 or 2 lines] Pressure-test it before I commit. 1. The hidden assumptions, and what this source gains if I say yes. 2. How it most likely fails for someone in my situation, including who tried this and isn't around to talk about it. 3. The strongest honest case for not doing this, argued by whoever would actually know. Someone who has done it, someone who has been in my position, or someone qualified in that field. 4. What evidence would change your answer. 5. The smallest low-risk test I can run today. If the advice is sound, say so plainly instead of inventing problems to find.
1006: 
1007:  Why it works: Telling it where the advice came from changes the answer. A contractor who profits from the job and a friend who has done it twice fail in different ways. Item 3 argues back as someone who would actually know, so the objection carries weight.
1008: 
1009:  One thing: It only sees what you paste. Give it your summary of the advice and it will pressure-test your summary.
1010: 
1011:  Simple fix: Paste the advice word for word, even if it runs long. Hit the dictation button & give it more context.

1051: Subject: A Prompt to Win a Yes & another that makes AI Prove its Sources
1052: Body:
1053: Plus a viral dev prompt that turns out it's not just for devs
1054: 
1055: How to Win a Yes, Make AI Prove Its Sources, & Grill Yourself Before You Build
1056: 
1057:  Plus the developer skill that turns out it's not just for devs
1058: 
1059:  Sponsored by
1060:  Charge clients $3K. Build their site in 10 minutes.
1061: 
1062:  AI freelancers use Readdy.ai to turn $2–5K website gigs into afternoon builds.
1063: 
1064:  Enter a client brief and get a polished, mobile-ready site with copy, SEO, booking, Stripe, and self-editing chat.
1065: 
1066:  White-label and export-friendly, Readdy helps you deliver faster, keep margins, and scale your freelance business.
1067: 
1068:  Start your next gig
1069: 
1070:  AI wants to look done.
1071: 
1072:  Ask it for anything & it hands you something finished. A tidy report, a confident script, a plan that's ready to run.
1073: 
1074:  It looks like real work got done.
1075: 
1076:  Some of it is. Some of it's fiction. You can't tell by looking.
1077: 
1078:  Every prompt this week makes it deliver facts. Show your work, cite the source, ask me before you run off & build.
1079: 
1080:  Turns out we're all back in grade school, checking work.
1081: 
1082:  This time we're the teacher. Seen This Week
1083:  The Prompt to Win a Yes Without Pushing
1084: 
1085:  It's Friday. You want out by 3 & the only person who can cover the desk is Sam.
1086: 
1087:  So you do the lazy thing. You open the chat & type "Come up with something good to convince Sam to cover for me."
1088: 
1089:  It writes, “3 reasons Sam should say yes”. A closer so sure of itself you almost laugh.
1090: 
1091:  You'd never say a word of it out loud. It sounds like a tele-marketer selling you life insurance.
1092: 
1093:  And we all know people typically agree more when the whole thing feels like their idea.
1094: 
1095:  That's why this prompt doesn't hand you a pitch.
1096: 
1097:  It builds around a question Sam answers, names the objection before they can & gives them 2 ways to say yes that work for everyone. 🤯 I need to get [person, like my manager or my partner] to [do the thing]. They haven't said yes yet. First, ask me 2 things, then wait for my answer: 1. How big is the ask, and have we disagreed about it before? 2. Who is this person to me, a partner, a coworker, a friend? The same words land differently depending on that. Then build the approach on how people actually agree to things: - Open with a calibrated question, one that starts with "how" or "what" and makes them help solve my problem ("how am I supposed to get this done by Friday and still cover the desk?"). Never one they can answer with a flat "no." - Name their likely objection before they raise it, so it loses its charge. - Give them 2 options that both work for me instead of one demand. People move faster when the choice feels like theirs. Give me 3 things I could actually say, shortest to longest, matched to who this person is to me. Tell me which to open with. Then a fallback if they still balk, the smallest yes that keeps things moving, not the whole ask at once.
1098: 
1099:  Why it works: It asks 2 questions before writing anything, so the ask fits the actual person instead of a stranger. The calibrated question hands them your problem to solve instead of something to push back on. Like 8-mile, naming the objection first takes the air out of it.
1100: 
1101:  One thing: That same move backfires if you guess the objection wrong. Tell Sam "you probably think this is too much to ask" & you've just handed them a reason they hadn't thought of.
1102: 
1103:  Simple fix: Tell it to open with the question & hold the objection line until you've heard their real one. Your Website Shouldn't Look Like It Was AI-Generated
1104: 
1105:  You know the pain. Your AI builder ships something functional. Technically a website. But your customers can tell.
1106: 
1107:  Readdy.ai generates designs that actually convert, with clean layouts, professional copy, real visual hierarchy, and distinct custom designs that don't look like AI.
1108: 
1109:  Get a site that's as special as your business. Live in under 5 minutes.
1110: 
1111:  Agency quality. DIY price.
1112: 
1113:  Build your site for free.
1114:  The Research Prompt that Makes it Cite its Source
1115: 
1116:  True story. Earlier this week I asked AI to compare 2 email platforms. Prices, features, & enough trade-offs to help me pick one.
1117: 
1118:  I had a clean report back in 39 seconds. So beautifully formatted I almost forwarded it to a friend.
1119: 
1120:  Then a source it cited caught my eye.
1121: 
1122:  Dead link.
1123: 
1124:  Tried another & that article was 2.5 years old, its prices long since sailed off into the sunset.
1125: 
1126:  Claude never opened a single site. It faked the report from the bits it already knew.
1127: 
1128:  Same way I faked book reports on the Odyssey in 9th grade.
1129: 
1130:  The fantasy sat shoulder to shoulder with the facts & I couldn't tell which was which.
1131: 
1132:  So I rebuilt the prompt from the ground up. It has to show its work now (when it can't, it tells on itself & marks the line unverified). You are my research assistant. Research the topic below and hand me a brief I can trust. Follow every rule; do not skip the retrieval rules. TOPIC: [drop your topic here] PURPOSE: [decision / presentation / just understanding] DEPTH: [quick scan / standard / deep] BEFORE YOU RESEARCH Turn my topic into the 3 specific questions worth answering. Show me the 3 questions first, then answer them. SOURCING RULES (these are the point of this prompt) 1. Cite inline. Put the real URL in parentheses right after each claim, not in a list at the end. 2. Retrieved only. State a fact only if you actually pulled it from a source in this session. If you can't verify it, write "Unverified:" in front of it. Never invent a URL, statistic, date, or quote. 3. Match the source to the claim: - Factual data (prices, specs, dates): the official/primary source is fine. Use the company's own page for its own numbers. - Opinion or comparison ("best," "better," "worth it"): independent third-party sources ONLY. A company can never be the source that says it is the best. 4. Triangulate anything that matters. For key numbers, check a second source. If a primary source and a third party disagree, show both and trust the primary for its own facts. 5. Date every source. Flag anything that looks stale. STANCE Stay neutral. Assume no preferred answer and do not tailor the verdict to me. If the honest answer is "it depends," say what it depends on. OUTPUT Query: [restate the exact question researched] The 3 questions: list them. TL;DR: 2-3 sentences. Findings: one short section per question, each factual claim carrying its inline source. Mark unverified items plainly. Where sources disagree: name the conflict and which you trust and why. Verdict: the neutral answer, third-party sources only. Confidence: rate each major finding High / Medium / Low, tied to whether you retrieved and corroborated it. Still open: what you couldn't verify.
1133: 
1134:  Why it works: It makes the model cite inline & only from sources it actually pulled up, so you can see which claims are real. It splits the sourcing rule the right way, ask a company for its own price, never for whether it's the best. When it can't verify something, it says so instead of making it up. The Teardown
1135:  The Viral Dev Prompt That Works on Anything
1136: 
1137:  There's a Claude skill on GitHub with over 174,000 stars & its dev, Matt Pocock, is still updating it.
1138: 
1139:  If you're a dev, you've probably seen /grill-me. It's part of a whole suite of skills he put out.
1140: 
1141:  If you had one guess at what this skill does, you'd probably get it right.
1142: 
1143:  The whole thing is wrapped around a single prompt & that prompt does all the heavy lifting. Which means you can run it on any model.
1144: 
1145:  Saves everybody a bucketful of time & headache before they burn a weekend building the wrong thing, only to get their hearts broken later on. Interview me relentlessly about every aspect of this plan until we reach a shared understanding. Walk down each branch of the design tree, resolving dependencies between decisions one-by-one. For each question, provide your recommended answer. If a question can be answered by exploring the codebase, explore the codebase instead. 
1146: 
1147:  Take that last line out and the prompt is wide open. Point it at a course, a product you can't position, a decision you keep circling.
1148: 
1149:  Then make it hand you a TLDR, because the AI talks more than a toddler on a sugar high. Especially Opus. Interview me relentlessly about [my plan or decision] until we reach a shared understanding. Walk down each branch of the decision tree, resolving dependencies one at a time. For each question, give me your recommended answer. Ask one question at a time and wait for my reply. Keep each turn short, and give me a TLDR at the top of any long answer. 
1150:

1180: Name: Alex Hormozi
1181: Subject: Mozi Minute: Big Head, Long Tail
1182: Body:
1183: Words I like: Motivation has an expiration date. Offer the most when motivation is highest.
1184: 
1185:  Mozi Minute: Big Head, Long Tail
1186: 
1187:  Many businesses offer trials and low-ticket offers. This is fine if your goal is automated conversion.
1188: 
1189:  We do it at Skool everyday - there's nothing wrong with it.
1190: 
1191:  But if you have a sales person - which 80% of you do...
1192: 
1193:  Do not start with a trial
1194: 
1195:  Your prospects are most excited about solving their problem the moment they decide to fix it.
1196: 
1197:  That's when you should charge the most.
1198: 
1199:  Not after a trial. Not after they cool off. Right then.
1200: 
1201:  The Big Head, Long Tail Model:
1202: 
1203:  Charge a lot upfront when motivation peaks. Then add lower-priced continuity on the backend. Big purchase happens when pain is highest. Recurring revenue comes after they're committed.
1204: 
1205:  Why This Crushes Trials: (Again, if you have a salesperson).
1206: 
1207:   * Offsets CAC Immediately
1208:  You get paid upfront.
1209: 
1210:  While competitors spend $300 to acquire someone paying $49/month (hoping they stick around), you collect $500-$1000 on day one. This means you can outspend them.
1211: 
1212:  They'll have to turn off their ad campaigns while you keep eating up market share.
1213: 
1214:   * Captures Peak Motivation
1215:  Someone drowning doesn't want swimming lessons.
1216: 
1217:  They want out of the water.
1218: 
1219:  When prospects are desperate, sell them the complete solution.
1220: 
1221:   * Gets Them More Invested
1222:  Big upfront payment = high commitment = better results.
1223: 
1224:  They show up. They do the work. They get results.
1225: 
1226:  It's in their best interest to get them to invest more in themselves.
1227: 
1228:  Your team will also enjoy working with more committed people.
1229: 
1230:   * Screens For Better Customers
1231:  People willing to pay $500-$1000 upfront are serious buyers.
1232: 
1233:  They have money. They have urgency.
1234: 
1235:  With trials, you'll get more tire kickers which can wear down staff.
1236: 
1237:   * Higher LTV, Lower Churn
1238:  Sunk cost bias works in your favor.
1239: 
1240:  After paying $1000 upfront, they're not canceling the $99/month membership.
1241: 
1242:  The continuity fee feels like nothing by comparison.
1243: 
1244:  Real Example:
1245:

1: # Voice Attributes
2: 
3: How to define, document, and validate the 3-5 voice attributes that anchor TONE.md. Voice is the brand's fixed personality — it does **not** change across channels. Tone modulates per situation; voice does not.
4: 
5: ---
6: 
7: ## Table of contents
8: 
9: - [The "X but never Y" pattern](#the-x-but-never-y-pattern)
10: - [Attribute documentation template](#attribute-documentation-template)
11: - [NN/g 4 dimensions](#nng-4-dimensions)
12: - [Jung's 12 archetypes](#jungs-12-archetypes)
13: - [BrandSort / message architecture](#brandsort--message-architecture)
14: - [Brand-as-person exercise](#brand-as-person-exercise)
15: - [Frameworks compared](#frameworks-compared)
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## The "X but never Y" pattern
20: 
21: The single most useful documentation device in the discipline. Slack's published voice:
22: 
23: > _"Confident (never cocky), Witty (but never silly), Conversational (but always appropriate and respectful), Intelligent (but not arrogant), Friendly (but not ingratiating), Helpful (never overbearing), Clear, concise and human."_
24: 
25: Why it works: every attribute carries its own anti-attribute. Writers learn what to do AND what to avoid in the same memorable phrase. Without the "never Y" half, "confident" reads as a synonym for "cocky" to half the team.
26: 
27: For each attribute, produce **three** "we are X but we are not Y" statements during the BrandSort exercise. The triplet forces specificity — by the third statement, generic phrasing collapses and concrete language emerges.
28: 
29: **Bad** (generic, won't survive use):
30: 
31: - "We are friendly."
32: - "We are professional."
33: 
34: **Good** (specific, falsifiable):
35: 
36: - "Confident, never cocky."
37: - "Plainspoken, not patronising."
38: - "Warm, but never saccharine."
39: 
40: ---
41: 
42: ## Attribute documentation template
43: 
44: Each attribute in TONE.md follows this exact structure (downstream skills parse on it):
45: 
46: ```
47: ### N. <Attribute name>
48: 
49: **Definition:** <one line — what this attribute means in practice>
50: 
51: **Sounds like:** "<one example sentence in the voice>"
52: 
53: **Does not sound like:** "<one anti-example — generic, off-brand, or category default>"
54: 
55: **Do:**
56: - <concrete behaviour 1>
57: - <concrete behaviour 2>
58: - <concrete behaviour 3>
59: 
60: **Don't:**
61: - <concrete behaviour 1>
62: - <concrete behaviour 2>
63: - <concrete behaviour 3>
64: 
65: **Anti-example from past content:** "<actual past sentence that violated this attribute>"
66: ```
67: 
68: **Why anti-examples from past content matter:** abstract anti-examples ("don't be too formal") fail to bite. Anti-examples sourced from the brand's own historical copy bite because writers recognise them — "oh, I wrote that exact sentence last quarter." This is where the guide stops being theatre and starts shaping behaviour.
69: 
70: ---
71: 
72: ## Worked attribute example
73: 
74: Drawn from a B2B SaaS context — adapt for the brand at hand.
75: 
76: ```
77: ### 1. Plainspoken
78: 
79: **Definition:** We say what we mean in the fewest credible words.
80: 
81: **Sounds like:** "Your invoice failed. Update your card to keep your subscription."
82: 
83: **Does not sound like:** "Unfortunately, we were unable to process the transaction at this time."
84: 
85: **Do:**
86: - Use active voice — name who does what.
87: - Lead with the most important fact.
88: - Use one idea per sentence.
89: 
90: **Don't:**
91: - Hedge ("perhaps", "potentially").
92: - Use insurance-language passives ("an error has occurred").
93: - Stack qualifiers ("we are currently unable to potentially process...").
94: 
95: **Anti-example from past content:** "It has come to our attention that, in some cases, certain customers may have experienced..."
96: ```
97: 
98: ---
99: 
100: ## NN/g 4 dimensions
101: 
102: Nielsen Norman Group's measurement layer for voice. Four spectra, each a 3-point scale (or 5-point if you want finer granularity):
103: 
104: | Dimension | One end | Other end | Default for most brands |
105: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
106: | Funny ↔ Serious | Funny | Serious | Lean serious; reserve funny for moments of relief |
107: | Formal ↔ Casual | Formal | Casual | Most modern brands lean casual |
108: | Respectful ↔ Irreverent | Respectful | Irreverent | Respectful unless the brand is Outlaw archetype |
109: | Enthusiastic ↔ Matter-of-fact | Enthusiastic | Matter-of-fact | Matter-of-fact for B2B trust; enthusiastic for D2C |
110: 
111: **Use case:** plot the brand on all four dimensions. Plot 3-5 competitors on the same chart. Look for clustering — if you're at the same coordinates as two competitors, your voice is not differentiating. Move at least one dimension.
112: 
113: **Anti-pattern:** clustering near the midpoint on all four dimensions. Per Quasa.io's diagnosis: _"teams defaulting to mid-range scores (4-7), result in bland, forgettable voices."_ If three dimensions are at midpoint, the brand has no voice.
114: 
115: **Empirically grounded:** NN/g research shows tone of voice measurably affects perceived friendliness, trustworthiness, and desirability. On average, **52% of the variability in desirability scores is explained by trustworthiness** — meaning trust-building tone dimensions (matter-of-fact, plainspoken, respectful) pay more than charm.
116: 
117: ---
118: 
119: ## Jung's 12 archetypes
120: 
121: Strategic personality alignment with audience psychology. Each archetype maps to a core motivation — pick the one whose audience your buyer most resembles.
122: 
123: | Archetype | Core motivation | Example brands |
124: | --- | --- | --- |
125: | **Innocent** | Safety, simplicity, optimism | Coca-Cola, Dove |
126: | **Sage** | Truth, knowledge, mastery | Stripe (docs), Harvard, BBC |
127: | **Explorer** | Freedom, discovery, autonomy | Patagonia, Jeep, REI |
128: | **Outlaw / Rebel** | Disruption, freedom, revolution | Harley-Davidson, Liquid Death, Oatly |
129: | **Magician** | Vision, transformation | Apple, Disney, Tesla |
130: | **Hero** | Mastery, courage, achievement | Nike, FedEx, Patagonia (also) |
131: | **Lover** | Intimacy, beauty, pleasure | Chanel, Godiva, Häagen-Dazs |
132: | **Jester** | Joy, play, mischief | Old Spice, Mailchimp, Duolingo (TikTok) |
133: | **Everyman** | Belonging, realism, equality | IKEA, Target, Budweiser |
134: | **Caregiver** | Service, compassion, protection | Johnson & Johnson, Volvo, charity: water |
135: | **Ruler** | Control, leadership, prosperity | Rolex, Mercedes-Benz, Microsoft (enterprise) |
136: | **Creator** | Self-expression, craft, innovation | Lego, Apple (also), Adobe |
137: 
138: **Use caveats:**
139: 
140: 1. Most brands lead with one archetype and borrow from one adjacent (e.g. Apple = Magician primary, Creator secondary).
141: 2. Archetype is a positioning shortcut, not a voice solution. Two "Hero" brands can sound completely different (Nike vs FedEx). Don't stop at the archetype label — derive concrete voice attributes from it.
142: 3. Brands that lean too hard on archetype end up in cosplay. The archetype should inform decisions, not become a costume.
143: 
144: ---
145: 
146: ## BrandSort / message architecture
147: 
148: Margot Bloomstein's exercise (_Content Strategy at Work_, Morgan Kaufmann, 2012) for surfacing brand attributes through a card-sort:
149: 
150: 1. Use a deck of ~100 brand-attribute adjective cards (or generate a list).
151: 2. Sort each card into one of three piles: **who we are now**, **who we'd like to be**, **who we are not**.
152: 3. Narrow the "who we'd like to be" pile to ~9 cards.
153: 4. Group those 9 into three clusters of three; pick the strongest from each cluster.
154: 5. The top 3 are the message architecture and the seed for voice attributes.
155: 
156: **Run with a cross-functional group of 6-10 people**: leadership, marketing, sales, customer success, product writing, support, HR. The disagreements between groups are diagnostic — surface them explicitly rather than averaging them out.
157: 
158: **Reconcile** by running BrandSort three times:
159: 
160: 1. Once with leadership
161: 2. Once with the writing team
162: 3. Once with sales / customer success (who hear how customers actually talk)
163: 
164: Differences between the three runs reveal where the brand's self-image diverges from its operational reality. Force a decision in the room rather than letting it persist as ambiguity in the guide.
165: 
166: ---
167: 
168: ## Brand-as-person exercise
169: 
170: A forcing function for concreteness. If the brand were a person at a dinner party:
171: 
172: - Job, age range, hobbies?
173: - What do they read?
174: - Who do they admire?
175: - How do they introduce themselves?
176: - What do they refuse to talk about?
177: - What do they wear?
178: 
179: For B2B brands, substitute "ideal colleague" or "celebrity spokesperson" — Slack explicitly aims to be _"an ideal colleague"_. This frames voice as a relationship the brand has with the reader, not an abstract personality.
180: 
181: **Output:** one paragraph describing this person. Then check: does the brand actually sound like this person in its current content? If not, that gap is what TONE.md is for.
182: 
183: ---
184: 
185: ## Frameworks compared
186: 
187: | Framework | What it gives you | Where it falls short |
188: | --- | --- | --- |
189: | **NN/g 4 dimensions** | Measurable axes; comparable profiles; falsifiable decisions | Misses culture and lexicon; can produce average outputs if everyone clusters near midpoint |
190: | **Mailchimp voice/tone** | Cleanest articulation of voice/tone distinction; mature documentation pattern | Specific to a SaaS context; not a discovery method |
191: | **Jung's 12 archetypes** | Strategic personality alignment; audience psychology link | Often used too literally; archetypes become cosplay |
192: | **"We are / We are not"** | Forces specificity; produces usable do/don't pairs | Easy to write trivially ("we are friendly but not unfriendly") if not facilitated |
193: | **Voice attributes with do/don't tables** | The operational atom of any modern guide | Without examples, becomes abstract |
194: | **Tone spectrums** (Builtvisible / Adobe Spectrum) | Channel-by-channel modulation made visible | Maintenance burden if too many spectrums |
195: | **Margot Bloomstein's BrandSort** | Stakeholder alignment; prioritised attributes; basis for content audit | Outputs are inputs; still need lexicon, examples, modulation matrix |
196: | **GV Brand Sprint (3 Circles)** | Speed; useful for early-stage startups | Lightweight; not a substitute for the full method |
197: 
198: **No single framework is sufficient.** Combine: BrandSort for stakeholder alignment, NN/g 4 dimensions for differentiation, "X but never Y" for documentation, archetype as positioning shortcut. Each addresses a different stage of the work.

1442:  Step 4: Find The Preventable Obstacles
1443: 
1444:  By the time you finish writing, you should have a clear view of the main obstacles ahead of you.
1445: 
1446:  Some you can prevent.
1447: 
1448:  Others you can't.

1451: 
1452:   * You can't prevent someone's childhood trauma from surfacing in a relationship, but you can prevent yourself feeling resentful by just telling them you don't want their fucking cat to move in.
1453: 
1454:   * You can't prevent a local asking you a random question in Spanish, but you can prevent yourself not being prepared enough for when the time comes.
1455: 
1456:   * You can't prevent releasing something and no one buying it (to an extent lol), but you can prevent overwhelming yourself with too many projects by never starting something new until you've finished the old thing.
1457:  Discovering the ones you can't prevent is the main reason people avoid this exercise.

1474:

1476: 
1477:   * Redesign it because the obstacles are manageable.

1479:   * Proceed because the desire survives contact with reality.

1589: 
1590:  For it to sink in though, you first need to understand something absurd.
1591: 
1592:  Here's what's really going on…
1593: 
1594:  You worry because your brain has convinced you it's helpful.
1595: 
1596:  Not because you're an “anxious person”.
1597: 
1598:  Just because your brain is convinced the more you worry the more you can see round dark corners.
1599: 
1600:  So, to your brain, worrying feels responsible.
1601: 
1602:  That's why stopping it feels like someone ripping your life jacket off.
1603: 
1604:  The truth…
1605: 
1606:  Worrying is just planning that never ends.
1607: 
1608:  Why this matters…
1609: 
1610:  Worrying, at the wrong time, is like letting the smoke alarm in your kitchen constantly ring out.
1611: 
1612:  Stress.
1613: 
1614:  Because constant worry keeps your nervous system in suspense; convinced trouble is just around the corner.
1615: 
1616:  You know… like… saber-tooth-tiger-kinda-trouble.
1617: 
1618:  That's why you have the general feeling that something's “off” - like someone is mad at you or something bad is about to happen any minute even while you're just pouring a bowl of cornflakes in your kitchen on a Tuesday morning.
1619: 
1620:  It's also why you feel like you've run a marathon even when you've been standing still for the last 10 minutes.
1621: 
1622:  Now before we dive into the solution, why bother being invested in it in the first place?
1623: 
1624:  The upsides of freeing yourself from constant worry…
1625: 
1626:  Your brain is always going to worry to some extent.
1627: 
1628:  But the upsides of reducing it - even slightly - are worth it and are best summarised like this:
1629: 
1630:  Imagine all the mental and physical energy that gets zapped when your brain focuses on imagined disaster.
1631: 
1632:  Now imagine all that energy being freed up for you to use.
1633: 
1634:  The result?
1635: 
1636:  You get your life back.
1637: 
1638:  Because you no longer have this vague gnawing ache that “my life is happening but I'm not really in it.”
1639: 
1640:  Instead, you can fully connect with whatever or whoever is in front of you; the partner, the friend, the deep work, the hobby.
1641: 
1642:  The result being; more peace, stillness, connection and joy.
1643: 
1644:  If that sounds worth it, you're ready to add the anti-worry protocol to your tool belt.
1645: 
1646:  When your mind is looping in the clouds, you need to let it LAND.
1647: 
1648:  Here's the first step.
1649: 
1650:  L - Label.
1651: 
1652:  You can't solve something you can't see.
1653: 
1654:  Which is why the first step in the protocol is to simply notice when your mind is busy, then label the experience to yourself out loud by saying:
1655: 
1656:  “Hmm, my mind is busy right now.”
1657: 
1658:  This works because when you become aware of your mind's busyness, you distance yourself from it - which stops you from identifying with the part of you that worries.
1659: 
1660:  Then, once you've labelled what's going on, you need to ask yourself a question...
1661: 
1662:  A - Ask.
1663: 
1664:  Earlier we said: your brain worries because it's convinced worrying is helpful.
1665: 
1666:  So to snap it out of that, you need to teach your brain the difference between what's helpful and what's not.
1667: 
1668:  In short…
1669: 
1670:  Planning is helpful.
1671: 
1672:  Worrying/looping beyond a plan being made, isn't.
1673: 
1674:  Personal example:
1675: 
1676:   * Late 2024 I was stuck, wanting to move country. I had 6 on my list, spent 6 months researching the pros and cons of each, but early 2025 I broke down from confusion. I had no idea what one to pick and no more thinking was helping. So one day I did a workout and said I'd leave the gym with a decision. An hour later I came back and booked my flights to Mexico. As soon as I pressed “book” and the screen refreshed to reveal "booking confirmed", my shoulders relaxed and I breathed a sigh of relief as I felt all the worry melt away.
1677:  To unpack that example, here's the deeper difference between the two, just let it sink in:
1678: 
1679:  Planning ends in:
1680: 
1681:   * A decision
1682: 
1683:   * A next action
1684: 
1685:   * A clearer path forward
1686:  It asks: what will I do?
1687: 
1688:  You can tell your brain is trying to usefully plan something because it'll reach a destination - each thought feeling like it's getting you closer.
1689: 
1690:  The result being you'll feel aligned, calm, clear, secure and your emotions will stop wobbling and start walking straight.
1691: 
1692:  On the other hand, worrying just replays danger without resolution.
1693: 
1694:  If useful planning helps your brain reach a destination, worrying keeps it lost in the woods. Where no new information helps, the emotions you don't want to feel ramp up and you just feel cloudy, foggy and as if your mind is trying to use a torn map with scribbles all over it.
1695: 
1696:  If planning asks: what will I do? worry asks: what if?
1697: 
1698:  The key takeaway…
1699: 
1700:  Planning ends, makes action possible and lets you relax.
1701: 
1702:  Worrying loops, stalls action and keeps your mind busy.
1703: 
1704:  So after you've noticed your mind is busy, simply ask yourself:
1705: 
1706:  Worrying or planning?
1707: 
1708:  This should be enough for you to see what's happening one layer deeper.
1709: 
1710:  And if you get the sense you're planning - your thinking is resulting in you feeling clearer - keep following that direction until you reach a good enough destination and close this open loop.
1711: 
1712:  But if you notice your mind looping the disaster (ie. worrying) to no use, here's the next and most crucial step of this whole protocol…
1713: 
1714:  N - Name.
1715: 
1716:  Looping is like a fire.
1717: 
1718:  The air it needs to keep burning is vagueness.
1719: 
1720:  That's why the easiest way to calm yourself down and reduce worry is to clarify exactly what fear has sparked the loop in the first place.
1721: 
1722:  So instead of looping: “what if everything goes wrong?!”
1723: 
1724:  Write down on one side of a column: “what am I actually afraid might happen?”
1725: 
1726:  Then, on a piece of paper or on your phone notes, in a middle column of a table write; "what could I do to prevent it?"
1727: 
1728:  And in the final column; "what could I do to repair it if it happened?"
1729: 
1730:  Then brainstorm 1-2 answers for the middle and final column.
1731: 
1732:  For example:
1733: 
1734:  Fear 1 = My partner is upset with me and our relationship is falling apart.
1735: 
1736:  Prevent = Ask them what's wrong and summarise their point back to them in my own words.
1737: 
1738:  Repair = Repair damage if possible. Have the difficult "are we still committed?" convo.
1739: 
1740:  Fear 2 = I never figure my life out and end up unhappy.
1741: 
1742:  Prevent = Focus on the next step instead of solving your entire future. Keep learning and taking action.
1743: 
1744:  Repair = Reassess direction. Make changes. Start again if needed. Most people reinvent themselves multiple times.
1745: 
1746:  Vague fears feel huge.
1747: 
1748:  Defined fears feel manageable.
1749: 
1750:  Before you move on, there's a final step that'll make sure your worry turns from lopping to action...
1751: 
1752:  D - Decide.
1753: 
1754:  So now you've named the fear, created prevention strategies and figured out a few ways to reverse it if it were to happen.
1755: 
1756:  The mistake would now be letting your mind say “great, let's loop it 30,000 times for the next 3 hours.”
1757: 
1758:  So what will actually close the loop and get this off your mind?
1759: 
1760:  The answer: a decision.
1761: 
1762:  Because remember earlier we said “worrying is just planning that never ends”.
1763:  Well in order to end it, you need to decide to stop planning.
1764:

1768: 
1769:  And instead, you're going to move forward with the information you have.
1770: 
1771:  Because the key thing to note is; the goal of planning isn't certainty. It's a decision.
