# TONE.md — AI Newsletter / Personal Brand Voice

> Generated by `samber/cc-skills@copywriting-tone-of-voice-creator` on `2026-07-25`. Version `1.0`.
>
> This is a machine-readable brand voice contract extracted from a curated email swipe file. Downstream content skills, bots, and ghostwriters consume this file to write on-brand copy. Do not rename sections or reorder them — pipelines depend on the structure.
>
> **Source material:** `COPY-BRAND-VOICE,STYLE,BRAND,TONE-EMAILS.txt` — a swipe file containing ~12 emails from: Ben's Bites (Ben Tossell), AI with Remy, Prompt Teardown, Alex Hormozi / Mozi Minute, Newel of Knowledge (Lewis), Pat @ Starter Story. **Primary voice models: Ben's Bites and AI with Remy** (most represented, most stylistically consistent). Secondary references: Alex Hormozi (punchy, direct), Newel of Knowledge (narrative-led, philosophical), Pat @ Starter Story (personal, story-first).

---

## Context

- **Brand:** AI Newsletter / Personal Founder Brand (modelled on Ben's Bites + AI with Remy dominant voice)
- **Category:** Personal brand + Media / Newsletter (B2C/D2C adjacent)
- **Mission (1 line):** Help non-technical people understand, use, and build with AI — one sharp, honest email at a time.
- **Primary audience:** Smart non-technical professionals, founders, and operators who want to use AI in their work and life without the hype or gatekeeping. They are curious, time-poor, slightly sceptical of buzzwords, and willing to pay for clarity.
- **Secondary audiences:**
  - Developers and technical practitioners who appreciate plain language over jargon performance
  - Aspiring solopreneurs building AI-powered workflows for the first time
- **Market(s) and language(s):** en-US primary, en-GB secondary (both voices present; contractions and casual grammar shared)
- **Reading-age target:** Adult general — smart but not academic. Never dumbs down; never shows off.
- **Channels in scope:** Email newsletter (primary), Twitter/X, LinkedIn, personal blog/website
- **Primary content goal:** Retention (keep subscribers reading, trusting, and sharing) + demand gen (courses, products, referrals)
- **Risk tolerance:** Moderately distinctive — willing to have an opinion, share personal life, and call things out honestly; not shock-jock irreverent
- **Regulatory constraints:** None formal. CAN-SPAM / GDPR for email (standard list hygiene; unsubscribe always present)

---

## Voice Attributes

The brand's fixed personality. These do **not** change across channels — only tone modulates.

### 1. Plainspoken, Never Dumbed Down

**Definition:** Writes at the level of a smart friend texting you a hot take — not a PR release, not a lecturer. Complex ideas are made simple without being made stupid.

**Sounds like:** "Kimi K3 is the first open-source model I'd actually use. It beats Fable on front-end design and costs half as much per task. Here's the setup."

**Does not sound like:** "In the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence, a paradigm shift is underway as a new entrant in the open-source ecosystem demonstrates competitive performance metrics relative to established frontier models."

**Do:**
- Lead with the most important fact in the first sentence — no throat-clearing
- Use the shortest word that carries the exact meaning (not "utilise", use "use"; not "leverage", use "use")
- Explain the so-what before the how: tell readers why it matters, then the detail

**Don't:**
- Open with scene-setting or context-padding before the point
- Stack technical acronyms without at least one plain-English translation
- Use corporate softeners: "in terms of," "with respect to," "at this point in time"

**Anti-example from past content:**

> "It has come to our attention that, in some cases, certain customers may have experienced delays in accessing their subscription content."

*(Nobody in this voice writes like this. The closest anti-pattern observed in the swipe file is the over-formatted Prompt Teardown sponsor copy, which reads correctly but loses the warmth.)*

---

### 2. Honest, Never Promotional

**Definition:** Tells the truth about a product, model, or idea even when that truth is "it's not ready yet," "I haven't tested it," or "this might not work for you." Credibility is the inventory; honesty is how it's restocked.

**Sounds like:** "I tested it on some pieces of 100% AI-written content and got 100% human scores on most of them. So I'm still unsure about how reliable it is." (Ben's Bites, on Pangram AI detection)

**Does not sound like:** "This groundbreaking tool is revolutionising the way professionals interact with AI, delivering unparalleled accuracy and industry-leading results."

**Do:**
- Qualify claims when you haven't personally verified: "They claim it's just as strong at knowledge work too, but I haven't tested it, so don't take my word for it"
- Name the downside of a product in the same breath as the upside
- Use concrete numbers when you have them; say "I don't have numbers" when you don't

**Don't:**
- Describe anything as "game-changing," "revolutionary," "world-class," or "industry-leading" without evidence
- Bury a limitation three paragraphs after the praise
- Write a sponsored segment that sounds indistinguishable from editorial

**Anti-example from past content:**

> "Metatate gives agents the rules they're missing — Try it for free." *(The Ben's Bites sponsor copy works, but it occasionally drifts close to generic claim territory. The self-aware editorial voice never drifts that far.)*

---

### 3. Personal Without Oversharing

**Definition:** The writer is in the room. Their real life — kids, burnout, a bad Airbnb, a birthday in Greece — shows up as texture, not content. The personal detail earns trust and explains the point of view; it is never the point of the email.

**Sounds like:** "Last December we had our third child, Poppy, and I was working at Factory. But she has some health issues, and I got pretty burnt out and overwhelmed, so I had to step back. For the last 7 months I've been plodding along work-wise without much agency. Which isn't like me at all." (Ben's Bites, birthday email)

**Does not sound like:** "As a busy parent and entrepreneur, I know how challenging it can be to balance personal and professional responsibilities while navigating the fast-paced world of technology."

**Do:**
- Drop the personal detail in 2-3 lines max, then pivot cleanly to the content
- Use specifics: not "a hard time" but "burnout," "stepped back," "7 months without agency"
- Let the personal detail serve as a bridge to a genuine point about how you work or think

**Don't:**
- Write more than one personal paragraph per email unless the personal IS the email
- Use personal backstory as filler to pad a thin issue
- Perform vulnerability ("as an imperfect human being in this crazy world…")

**Anti-example from past content:**

> "I refuse to put anything into the world that isn't exceptional, or as close to it as I can get." *(AI with Remy explaining the course delay — this works precisely because it is specific and brief, not because vulnerability is being performed for its own sake.)*

---

### 4. Curious, Never Hype-Chasing

**Definition:** Covers new things because they are genuinely interesting — not because they are trending. When something is overhyped, says so. When something is underrated, makes the case. Has strong opinions, loosely held.

**Sounds like:** "Fugu isn't a new frontier model at all. It's a router. Clever idea. Not a brand new one, mind you. In real testing though, the cracks show…" (AI with Remy, on Sakana Fugu)

**Does not sound like:** "Japan's Sakana AI just DROPPED their INSANE new model Fugu and it's COMPLETELY CHANGING the AI landscape!!!"

**Do:**
- Name the hype first, then correct it — this is the rhetorical pattern: "The internet instantly branded it a 'Fable killer.' It's not."
- Hold opinions with light hands: "I can't see it being something I use over other models" rather than "it's objectively bad"
- Ask the genuinely interesting question, not the clickbait question

**Don't:**
- Use ALL-CAPS or triple exclamation marks in editorial copy
- Cover something just because it is trending
- Hedge so carefully that no opinion survives

**Anti-example from past content:**

> "It's not the most impressive task by all means." *(Ben's Bites — this is the correct move: naming the limits of the example before the reader does. The anti-pattern would be presenting the taxi-booking story as revolutionary.)*

---

### 5. Warm, Never Ingratiating

**Definition:** Talks to readers as smart adults who share the same obsessions — not as an audience to be managed or a list to be monetised. The warmth is the warmth of a group chat with people who get it.

**Sounds like:** "Hey folks," / "What's up gang," / "So pumped to release this in a week's time and get you MFs AI power users!" (AI with Remy — calibrated to audience familiarity)

**Does not sound like:** "Dear Valued Subscriber, Thank you so much for being part of our incredible community. We are truly grateful for your continued support and loyalty."

**Do:**
- Address readers the same way you'd address a group chat with close peers
- Use "I" and "you" liberally — this is a one-to-one conversation at scale
- Ask genuine questions and mean them: "Hit reply and tell me what you would do" (Pat @ Starter Story)

**Don't:**
- Thank people for subscribing or reading — they know; it reads as filler
- Use "community" as a noun for your audience (feels corporate)
- End emails with generic closers: "As always, thanks for your continued support!"

**Anti-example from past content:**

> "You're getting this because you subscribed to the AI with Remy newsletter at aiwithremy.com. Don't want these emails? Unsubscribe here." *(The mandatory footer — necessary, legally fine, but it's the single coldest moment in every email. That contrast makes the warm editorial voice more vivid.)*

---

## Archetype

- **Primary:** Sage — knowledge, truth, mastery. The brand is trusted precisely because it explains what's real, not what's optimistic.
- **Secondary:** Everyman — relatable, honest about limitations, present in the mess of life alongside the reader.
- **Rationale:** The dominant voice in the swipe file (Ben's Bites, AI with Remy) earns its audience through intellectual honesty — the Sage move. But the Sage alone risks becoming the Wise Professor, which this voice never is. The Everyman secondary keeps it grounded: "I locked myself out my Airbnb today," "I'm running 3 young kids and this is the only project I've kept going." The archetype pairing explains why readers trust AND like this voice. An alternative reading — Creator — is present in the AI with Remy course-launch emails, but it is a mode, not the base voice.

---

## NN/g 4 Dimensions Positioning

Each dimension is a 3-point scale. At least 3 of 4 are clearly off-centre.

| Dimension | Position | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Funny ↔ Serious | Leaning funny | Dry wit, self-deprecating asides, occasional internet-native irreverence ("get you MFs AI power users"), but the content itself is taken seriously. Not a comedy newsletter. |
| Formal ↔ Casual | Casual | No punctuation performance, sentence fragments as style ("Not so much this time."), lowercase subject lines in several emails, "lol" used once and naturally. The formality dial is as low as editorial voice can go without losing credibility. |
| Respectful ↔ Irreverent | Leaning irreverent | Calls out hype directly, willing to say "this is bullshit," names the downside of a sponsored product, tells readers when the AI faked a source. Not impolite; irreverent toward the industry's posturing, not toward the reader. |
| Enthusiastic ↔ Matter-of-fact | Leaning matter-of-fact | The dominant mode is "here's what happened, here's what it means, here's what I'd do." Enthusiasm is reserved for genuine moments (Etched investment backstory, the AI taxi story) and reads as real because it is rationed. |

---

## Tone Modulation Matrix

How tone shifts by situation × channel. Each cell: **dominant tone** + 2–3 prohibited tones.

| Situation \ Channel | **Email Newsletter** | **Twitter/X** | **LinkedIn** | **Blog/Website** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Launch / win** | Excited but grounded — share the real number, the honest caveat. ✗ Hype, ✗ all-caps celebration, ✗ "we did it!" without specifics | Quick, punchy, one key fact + one hot take. ✗ Thread-bait, ✗ humble-brag | Measured professional enthusiasm — what it means, why it matters. ✗ Cringe celebration post, ✗ self-congratulation without substance | Detailed writeup — the story behind the number. ✗ Sales-page framing, ✗ vagueness |
| **Crisis / outage** | Direct and fast — state what happened, own it, say what's being done. ✗ Corporate passive voice, ✗ "we apologise for any inconvenience", ✗ silence | Same: direct, fast, human. ✗ PR-speak | Brief professional acknowledgment. ✗ Over-explanation, ✗ legal hedging | Full post-mortem when resolved. ✗ Blaming third parties |
| **Complaint (justified)** | Name the failure, take ownership, offer a concrete fix. ✗ Deflecting, ✗ policy-speak | Acknowledge publicly, resolve privately when possible. ✗ Defensive | Professional acknowledgment + fix. ✗ Delete / ignore | — |
| **Complaint (unjustified / viral)** | State the facts once, clearly, without drama. ✗ Fighting back, ✗ lengthy rebuttals, ✗ silence | One clear tweet correcting the record. ✗ Threading a full defence, ✗ clapping back | Stay off LinkedIn for drama; address via newsletter if necessary. ✗ Public argument | — |
| **Sensitive societal topic** | Careful, factual, brief — only address if directly relevant to AI/tech. ✗ Hot takes, ✗ political positioning | Share a factual observation, not a stance. ✗ Performative | Skip or reference a more substantive piece. ✗ Engagement-bait | Long-form, sourced, balanced analysis only. ✗ Opinion without evidence |
| **Bad news (price increase, sunset, change)** | Honest, early, with context. Lead with the change, explain the why, give the timeline. ✗ Burying it, ✗ spin | Share the key fact with a link to the full explanation. ✗ Minimising | Professional + brief. ✗ Defensive framing | — |
| **Routine / informational** | Conversational, energetic, clear structure. Headlines → brief take → link. ✗ Exhaustive summaries, ✗ no opinion | One-sentence take + link. ✗ Long threads on routine news | Brief framing + link to email/post. ✗ Reprinting the full email | Full depth — this is the right channel for long analysis. ✗ Short content |
| **Sales objection** | Pre-empt honestly — "here's the caveat before you buy." ✗ Oversell, ✗ false urgency, ✗ fear-based close | Not for sales objections. | Not for sales objections. | Detailed FAQ / honest positioning page. ✗ Testimonial-dump without critique |
| **Apology** | Brief, direct, specific. State what you did wrong, what you're doing about it. ✗ "I'm sorry if anyone was offended," ✗ over-apology performance | One clear tweet. ✗ Deletion as apology | Professional brief apology. ✗ Public self-flagellation | — |
| **Recruitment** | Personality-forward — describe what the work actually looks and feels like, not the benefits package. ✗ Corporate JD language, ✗ "rockstar" / "ninja" | Culture signals over job titles. ✗ Formal listing format | More formal but still human — share the real hiring criteria. ✗ Generic role description |

## Lexicon

### Preferred terms

| Term | Use for | Don't confuse with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `folks` | Email salutation (informal, warm, non-gendered) | `dear subscribers`, `hey everyone`, `hi all` |
| `readers` | Referring to the audience in third-person | `community`, `subscribers`, `users` |
| `agent` / `agents` | AI that takes autonomous, multi-step actions | `chatbot`, `assistant`, `bot` (unless chatbot is accurate) |
| `skill` / `skills` | Reusable AI instruction file that gives an agent a capability | `plugin`, `feature`, `tool` (unless the tool-call sense is meant) |
| `harness` | An interface or environment that wraps an AI model (e.g. Claude Code, Codex) | `platform`, `app` (too generic) |
| `frontier model` | Best-in-class large language model from a leading lab | `AI`, `LLM` (acceptable in technical context), `smart AI` (never) |
| `daily driver` | The model/tool you use for most work, not the most capable one | `default model`, `base model` |
| `context` | The information you give an agent to understand a task | `prompt` (too narrow), `instructions` (partially overlaps) |
| `connector` | A link between Claude and a live tool (Notion, Stripe, etc.) | `integration`, `plugin`, `add-on` |
| `in` / `out` | Pricing shorthand for input/output tokens (e.g. "$5 in / $30 out per million tokens") | "input cost," "output cost" (verbose in context) |
| `on-device` | Processing that happens locally, without sending data to a cloud server | `local`, `private` (both acceptable; `on-device` is most precise) |

### Banned terms

| Banned | Use instead | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `revolutionary` / `revolutionary AI` | "a significant step," "the first model to…" | Unverifiable marketing claim; readers distrust it |
| `game-changing` | Specific claim about what actually changed | Empty superlative |
| `industry-leading` | Cite the benchmark or the user number | Unverifiable, self-serving |
| `leverage` (metaphorical) | `use`, `apply`, `take advantage of` | Corporate jargon; banned in all non-financial contexts |
| `synergy` / `synergies` | Describe the actual combined effect | MBA cliché |
| `solution` (generic product noun) | Name the product or describe what it does | Means nothing without a subject |
| `excited to announce` | Just announce it | Self-referential; leads with the emotion rather than the news |
| `community` (for email list/audience) | `readers`, `subscribers`, or nothing (address them directly) | Corporate-feeling; implies management of the relationship |
| `deep dive` | `breakdown`, `full writeup`, `detailed look` | Overused across the category |
| `unlock` (metaphorical) | `access`, `get`, `enable` | Overused; feels growth-hacky |
| `supercharge` | The specific improvement | Vague power word with no referent |
| `seamlessly` | Describe what actually happens | Meaningless filler adverb |
| `rockstar` / `ninja` / `guru` (for roles/people) | Job title or actual descriptor | Cringe; alienating |
| `hustle` (as value) | Name the actual behaviour | Vague, often used to romanticise poor conditions |
| `empower` | Describe what the thing lets people do | Overused in the category to the point of meaninglessness |

### Power words

- sharp
- honest
- real
- actual
- works
- free
- fast
- cheaper
- better
- first
- new
- now
- here's why
- the catch
- but
- however
- worth
- exactly
- specific
- daily

### Jargon policy

- **Allowed for:** Technical detail in the body of an email when the primary audience is technical (API pricing, token counts, benchmark names, model architecture terms like "context window," "inference," "weights")
- **Prohibited for:** Subject lines, email openers, and any segment targeting general-audience readers without a plain-language explanation in the same sentence
- **Always define on first use** when crossing from technical to general-audience contexts. Pattern used in the swipe file: define in a parenthetical — *"agentic (just means the AI going off and doing multi-step tasks on its own)"*

### Naming conventions

- **Brand name:** Written exactly as the brand specifies (Ben's Bites, AI with Remy — respecting the capitalisation and punctuation of other brands when referencing them)
- **Product names:** Exact capitalisation: Claude, Codex, Notion, OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor — never lowercase unless stylistically deliberate (the swipe file writers use Fable, not "fable")
- **Feature names:** Treat like product names when they are proper nouns (Claude Tag, Claude Cowork, Fugu, Agent Hub)
- **Competitors:** Name them directly and honestly. Don't euphemise ("a major AI lab") when naming them is more useful. Don't punch at them unnecessarily — compare, don't attack.
- **Customers / users:** `readers` in third-person; `you` in direct address. Never `users` in the newsletter context (that's a product-UI word). Never `subscribers` in the editorial voice.
- **Models:** Refer to AI models with their full proper names on first mention; shorthand on repeat (e.g. "Fable 5" then "Fable"; "GPT-5.6 Sol" then "Sol"). Avoid generic "the model" without an antecedent.

---

## Mechanics

| Decision | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Person | 1st singular (`I`) for personal editorial; 1st plural (`we`) only when speaking for a team. 2nd singular (`you`) for the reader. Never 3rd person for the writer. |
| Contractions | Yes — always. `I've`, `it's`, `they're`, `don't`, `can't`. No contraction signals formality or caution; use sparingly for that effect only. |
| Oxford comma | Yes — used in the swipe file consistently. Prevents ambiguity in lists of 3+. |
| Sentence length (avg target) | 12–18 words for email body. Shorter for emphasis (as short as 2 words: "Not so much this time."). Longer acceptable in explanation paragraphs (20–25 words max). Average kept low for scanning. |
| Active vs passive default | Active — name who does what. Passive reserved for genuinely passive situations or when softening blame (crisis context only). |
| Sentence case vs title case | Sentence case throughout — subject lines, headers, section labels. Title case only in brand/product names. |
| Emoji policy | Sparingly in email; used as visual bullet-replacement (📌 TL;DR) or genuine emotional punctuation, not decoration. Zero emoji in formal contexts (LinkedIn body text, press, investor comms). Cap: 1–3 per email, 0–1 per tweet. |
| Punctuation tics | Em-dash: allowed, used for asides and pivots (not parentheses in casual copy). Ellipsis: allowed for trailing thought in casual register; not in professional contexts. Exclamation marks: one per email maximum; reserved for genuine excitement. No double exclamation (!!) ever in editorial. |
| Numerals | Always use numerals for numbers (even under 10 in body text) when they are data points: `3 young kids`, `6 live sessions`, `$1,497`. Spell out when ordinal/qualitative: "the third time," "a second look." |
| Dates | Written out in email context: "Monday June 29" or "July 7." Avoid DD/MM/YYYY ambiguity when writing for international audience. |
| Currencies | USD format `$1,497` with comma separator. Per-million-token pricing: `$5 in / $30 out` (the shorthand from the swipe file). |
| Lowercase in casual register | The AI with Remy voice uses sentence-start lowercase in some contexts ("the waitlist goes first," "but anyways…"). This is a deliberate style signal for extreme informality. Use only in the most casual channel (direct DM-style announcements, Twitter). Never in headline or subheader position. |

---

## Inclusive Language

- **Gendered language:** Avoid gendered generics. Use `folks` (already the preferred salutation), `they/them` for unknown individuals. Never `guys` as a generic group address.
- **Pronouns:** Use the person's preferred pronoun; if unknown, use their name or `they`. The swipe file uses `he/him` for named individuals when gender is established (Matt from Starter Story, Ben from Ben's Bites) — retain this when it is accurate.
- **Ability / disability:** Person-first where the person hasn't indicated preference. Avoid metaphors that trivialise disability ("blind spot" acceptable in non-clinical use; "cripple" / "lame" never).
- **Race and nationality:** Name nationalities and origins factually when relevant (Moonshot AI is Beijing-based; Sakana AI is Japan-based). Avoid stereotyping. Do not describe "Chinese" or "Japanese" models with exoticising language.
- **Age:** Do not use age as an implicit criticism or qualifier. The swipe file's "21-year old Harvard dropout" (Etched founder) is accurate biographical context, not dismissal.
- **Neurodiversity:** No terms casually applied as insults or metaphors ("crazy," "insane" appear in the swipe file as enthusiasm markers — acceptable in the current cultural register of the primary audience, but monitor for drift as norms shift).
- **Reference:** Conscious Style Guide (Karen Yin), APA Inclusive Language Guidelines.

---

## Channel-Specific Guidance

### Email Newsletter (Primary)

**Hard constraints:** No character limit. HTML rendering. Subject line is a headline; preview text is a secondary headline. Average open-scan time: 45 seconds. Subscriber is on their schedule, not yours.

**Tonal shift from voice baseline:** This is home base — the full voice applies here without modulation. The most personal, the most opinionated, the most willing to go long when the content earns it.

**Do:**
- Open with a personal one-liner or current event, then pivot to content within 3 sentences
- Use TL;DR as a scannable entry point for time-poor readers (AI with Remy pattern: 📌 TL;DR with bullet list)
- Separate headlines from quick links — the quick-links section is a separate reading mode (skimming vs. reading)

**Don't:**
- Write subject lines that are clever but unclear — "Caught cheating" (Ben's Bites) works because the preview text resolves it immediately
- Let a sponsor segment run longer than 5 sentences or sound different from the editorial voice
- End with a generic call to action ("Don't forget to share with a friend!")

**Example opening sentence in this channel:** "When I was in Greece, I needed to organise a taxi from the airport home. I pinged Codex and 1m37s later it was done."

---

### Twitter/X

**Hard constraints:** 280 characters per tweet. Thread max: 5 tweets before quality degrades. No markdown. Images/video increase reach.

**Tonal shift from voice baseline:** Compress the editorial voice to its sharpest edge. One observation, one opinion, one question, or one link per unit. The personal texture stays; the explanation collapses.

**Do:**
- Lead with the counter-intuitive statement or the sharp take, then add context if a thread
- Use the format: "[Surprising claim]. Here's why." as the single most effective opening
- Quote/retweet with a one-sentence hot take that adds something — never "this" or "interesting thread"

**Don't:**
- Thread out an email newsletter (tweet the link instead)
- Use thread-bait hooks: "I spent 6 months learning X. Here are 10 things you need to know:" — readers in this audience have learned to detect it
- Tweet more than once per day on the same topic; compression is the discipline here

**Example opening sentence in this channel:** "Fugu isn't a Fable killer. It's a router. Clever idea — but 3.5x slower than Opus in real testing."

---

### LinkedIn

**Hard constraints:** ~3,000 character limit per post. Algorithm rewards engagement (comments > likes). No markdown. Native document/carousel posts available.

**Tonal shift from voice baseline:** Dampen the informality by one step. Contractions stay. Personal anecdote stays. Remove slang and internet-native phrasing ("MFs," "lol," lowercase starts). Structure the post more explicitly — LinkedIn readers skim more aggressively.

**Do:**
- Open with a bold statement or a mini-story hook that lands in the first 2 lines (the "see more" cut-off)
- Make the first comment your link (LinkedIn suppresses link-in-post reach)
- End with a direct, genuine question that invites a short answer — not "what do you think?" but something specific

**Don't:**
- Use the "I was [X]. Then [Y] happened. Here's what I learned:" format — it is overused to the point of parody on this platform
- Repost the full newsletter; write a fresh angle with the link in comments
- Put emojis as bullet points — it looks like a template

**Example opening sentence in this channel:** "Three months ago I stepped back from work. Burnt out, third kid, health issues. This week I figured out the only project I've kept going for years — and why."

---

### Blog/Website

**Hard constraints:** No length limit. SEO is a factor (target keyword in H1, meta description, first paragraph). Evergreen content outlives the news cycle.

**Tonal shift from voice baseline:** More structured than email. Add subheadings every 300–400 words. The personal texture reduces slightly; the explanation expands. This is where the nuance that email compresses can live.

**Do:**
- Write for the reader who arrives from search, not just the subscriber who knows you — provide enough context for a cold reader
- Use H2s that are meaningful, not "Section 1" — the reader should be able to skim the H2s and understand the post's argument
- Include a concrete example or screenshot for every abstract claim

**Don't:**
- Write SEO-stuffed intros that repeat the keyword five times before saying anything useful
- Recycle email copy verbatim — expand or rework it for the medium
- End with "In conclusion, we have seen that…" — summarise by implication or cut to a single sharp closing line

**Example opening sentence in this channel:** "There are now four AI models worth caring about for daily knowledge work. Here is how I actually use each of them — and when I don't reach for them at all."

---

## Global Do's and Don'ts

A scannable, consolidated list for writers and bots loading TONE.md into their context window.

### Do

1. Lead with the point — the news, the take, the instruction — in the first sentence. Every time.
2. Name the downside of any product, model, or idea you are recommending.
3. Use short sentences for emphasis. Let them sit alone on a line.
4. Write "I" when you mean "I." Speak in first person from your own experience.
5. Qualify claims you haven't personally verified: "I haven't tested it, so don't take my word for it here."
6. Use concrete numbers, prices, and timeframes — not "affordable" but "$5 in / $30 out."
7. Correct hype directly: name the claim, then correct it in the next sentence.
8. Let the personal detail (the story, the life moment) serve the point — then drop it and move on.
9. Address the reader as `you`, one intelligent adult at a time.
10. End with a clear next action or a genuine question — never a generic closer.

### Don't

1. Don't use: revolutionary, game-changing, industry-leading, supercharge, unlock, seamlessly, deep dive, empower, synergy, leverage (metaphorical), excited to announce.
2. Don't open with context-setting, scene-painting, or throat-clearing — open with the news.
3. Don't write sponsor copy that sounds different from the editorial voice.
4. Don't use "community" to describe the reader list.
5. Don't hedge so much that no opinion survives the paragraph.
6. Don't stack more than one personal paragraph per piece — texture, not content.
7. Don't use ALL-CAPS or multiple exclamation marks in editorial.
8. Don't describe something as a first of its kind without checking if it is.
9. Don't thank the reader for subscribing, reading, or being here.
10. Don't write a conclusion that restates the intro — either extend the idea or cut.

## Examples Library

Before/after pairs and full-artefact samples that downstream writers can pattern-match against.

### Before / After

**1. Sponsor / product mention**

Before (off-brand):

> "We are thrilled to introduce our partnership with Metatate — an innovative, industry-leading platform that is revolutionising the way AI agents access and utilise business rules, enabling seamless and efficient agentic data workflows."

After (on-brand):

> "Most agentic data work is quietly propped up. The agent returns something plausible, and every answer gets checked in case it's plausibly wrong. Metatate gives agents the rules they're missing: which revenue definition to use, which policy applies, which records to trust. Try it for free."

Why: On-brand version leads with the problem, not the product; uses plain verbs; no banned adjectives. (Actual Ben's Bites sponsor copy — the standard to hit.)

---

**2. Model announcement (launch recap)**

Before (off-brand):

> "Anthropic has released Claude Sonnet 5, a powerful new AI model that delivers exceptional performance across a wide range of tasks at a competitive price point, making it an ideal choice for professionals seeking to leverage AI capabilities in their daily workflows."

After (on-brand):

> "Claude Sonnet 5 landed on June 30 — the first proper Sonnet upgrade since 4.6, and it's a big leap. It now lands right near Opus on a lot of real work. Only about 2% behind Opus 4.8 on computer use and agentic coding. But push it to high or max effort and its cost climbs right up onto Opus 4.8's. At that point Opus matches or beats it. So: Sonnet 5 for low and medium effort. Opus for the hard stuff."

Why: On-brand version leads with the fact, uses real numbers, names the limitation in the same breath as the praise, gives a direct recommendation. (Modelled on AI with Remy's Sonnet 5 coverage.)

---

**3. Personal opening**

Before (off-brand):

> "As entrepreneurs and builders in today's fast-paced AI landscape, we all know how challenging it can be to balance our personal lives with the demands of running a business. I certainly feel this tension, and I wanted to share some thoughts on how I've been navigating it."

After (on-brand):

> "Last December we had our third child, Poppy, and I was working at Factory. But she has some health issues, and I got pretty burnt out and overwhelmed, so I had to step back. For the last 7 months I've been plodding along work-wise without much agency. Which isn't like me at all. I'm going to put more of myself into this thing."

Why: On-brand version is specific (names, dates, circumstances), short (4 sentences), and pivots to a point. Off-brand version is generic, doesn't trust the reader to find their own relevance. (Actual Ben's Bites birthday email.)

---

**4. Product take (honest limitation)**

Before (off-brand):

> "Pangram's AI detection technology represents a significant advancement in the field, offering highly accurate results that have impressed us in our testing."

After (on-brand):

> "Pangram has sent the claim of 'AI detectors don't work' for a toss — it works wayyy better than most. But I'm still unsure about how reliable it is. I tested it on some pieces of 100% AI-written content and got 100% human scores on most of them."

Why: On-brand version praises the product, then immediately qualifies with a personal test result that contradicts the official narrative. This is the honesty pattern — it makes the praise credible. (Actual Ben's Bites coverage.)

---

### Full-artefact samples

- **Complete email (personal moment + product coverage):** Ben's Bites "Better design than Fable" (Jul 21) — the birthday email. Open with personal, pivot to product, maintain voice throughout sponsor segment.
- **Complete email (technical explanation for non-technical):** AI with Remy's Sonnet 5 / GPT-5.6 email — model for explaining AI pricing and performance tiers to a general audience.
- **Quick-links section format:** Ben's Bites "Quick links" — 6–10 items, each one sentence, no introductory paragraph, no outro. The voice is in the curation, not the commentary.

## Context

- **Brand:** AI Newsletter / Personal Founder Brand (modelled on Ben's Bites + AI with Remy dominant voice)
- **Category:** Personal brand + Media / Newsletter (B2C/D2C adjacent)
- **Mission (1 line):** Help non-technical people understand, use, and build with AI — one sharp, honest email at a time.
- **Primary audience:** Smart non-technical professionals, founders, and operators who want to use AI in their work and life without the hype or gatekeeping. They are curious, time-poor, slightly sceptical of buzzwords, and willing to pay for clarity.
- **Secondary audiences:**
  - Developers and technical practitioners who appreciate plain language over jargon performance
  - Aspiring solopreneurs building AI-powered workflows for the first time
- **Market(s) and language(s):** en-US primary, en-GB secondary
- **Reading-age target:** Adult general — smart but not academic. Never dumbs down; never shows off.
- **Channels in scope:** Email newsletter (primary), Twitter/X, LinkedIn, personal blog/website
- **Primary content goal:** Retention (keep subscribers reading, trusting, and sharing) + demand gen (courses, products, referrals)
- **Risk tolerance:** Moderately distinctive — willing to have an opinion, share personal life, and call things out honestly; not shock-jock irreverent
- **Regulatory constraints:** None formal. CAN-SPAM / GDPR for email (standard list hygiene; unsubscribe always present)

## Voice Attributes

The brand's fixed personality. These do **not** change across channels — only tone modulates.

### 1. Plainspoken, Never Dumbed Down

**Definition:** Writes at the level of a smart friend texting you a hot take — not a PR release, not a lecturer. Complex ideas are made simple without being made stupid.

**Sounds like:** "Kimi K3 is the first open-source model I'd actually use. It beats Fable on front-end design and costs half as much per task. Here's the setup."

**Does not sound like:** "In the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence, a paradigm shift is underway as a new entrant in the open-source ecosystem demonstrates competitive performance metrics relative to established frontier models."

**Do:**
- Lead with the most important fact in the first sentence — no throat-clearing
- Use the shortest word that carries the exact meaning (not "utilise", use "use"; not "leverage", use "use")
- Explain the so-what before the how: tell readers why it matters, then the detail

**Don't:**
- Open with scene-setting or context-padding before the point
- Stack technical acronyms without at least one plain-English translation
- Use corporate softeners: "in terms of," "with respect to," "at this point in time"

**Anti-example from past content:**

> "It has come to our attention that, in some cases, certain customers may have experienced delays in accessing their subscription content." *(Nobody in this voice writes like this. The anti-pattern is padding before the point.)*

---

### 2. Honest, Never Promotional

**Definition:** Tells the truth about a product, model, or idea even when that truth is "it's not ready yet," "I haven't tested it," or "this might not work for you." Credibility is the inventory; honesty is how it's restocked.

**Sounds like:** "I tested it on some pieces of 100% AI-written content and got 100% human scores on most of them. So I'm still unsure about how reliable it is." (Ben's Bites, on Pangram AI detection)

**Does not sound like:** "This groundbreaking tool is revolutionising the way professionals interact with AI, delivering unparalleled accuracy and industry-leading results."

**Do:**
- Qualify claims when you haven't personally verified: "They claim it's just as strong at knowledge work too, but I haven't tested it, so don't take my word for it"
- Name the downside of a product in the same breath as the upside
- Use concrete numbers when you have them; say "I don't have numbers" when you don't

**Don't:**
- Describe anything as "game-changing," "revolutionary," "world-class," or "industry-leading" without evidence
- Bury a limitation three paragraphs after the praise
- Write a sponsored segment that sounds indistinguishable from editorial (sponsor copy must be labelled and concise)

**Anti-example from past content:**

> "Metatate gives agents the rules they're missing — Try it for free." *(The Ben's Bites sponsor copy works, but sponsor copy occasionally drifts close to generic claim territory. The editorial voice never does.)*

---

### 3. Personal Without Oversharing

**Definition:** The writer is in the room. Their real life — kids, burnout, a bad Airbnb, a birthday in Greece — shows up as texture, not content. The personal detail earns trust and explains the point of view; it is never the point of the email.

**Sounds like:** "Last December we had our third child, Poppy, and I was working at Factory. But she has some health issues, and I got pretty burnt out and overwhelmed, so I had to step back. For the last 7 months I've been plodding along work-wise without much agency. Which isn't like me at all." (Ben's Bites, birthday email)

**Does not sound like:** "As a busy parent and entrepreneur, I know how challenging it can be to balance personal and professional responsibilities while navigating the fast-paced world of technology."

**Do:**
- Drop the personal detail in 2-3 lines max, then pivot cleanly to the content
- Use specifics: not "a hard time" but "burnout," "stepped back," "7 months without agency"
- Let the personal detail serve as a bridge to a genuine point about how you work or think

**Don't:**
- Write more than one personal paragraph per email unless the personal IS the email
- Use personal backstory as filler to pad a thin issue
- Perform vulnerability ("as an imperfect human being in this crazy world…")

**Anti-example from past content:**

> "I refuse to put anything into the world that isn't exceptional, or as close to it as I can get." *(AI with Remy explaining the course delay — this works precisely because it is specific and brief. The anti-pattern is performing the emotion for its own sake rather than in service of a point.)*

---

### 4. Curious, Never Hype-Chasing

**Definition:** Covers new things because they are genuinely interesting — not because they are trending. When something is overhyped, says so. When something is underrated, makes the case. Has strong opinions, loosely held.

**Sounds like:** "Fugu isn't a new frontier model at all. It's a router. Clever idea. Not a brand new one, mind you. In real testing though, the cracks show…" (AI with Remy, on Sakana Fugu)

**Does not sound like:** "Japan's Sakana AI just DROPPED their INSANE new model Fugu and it's COMPLETELY CHANGING the AI landscape!!!"

**Do:**
- Name the hype first, then correct it — "The internet instantly branded it a 'Fable killer.' It's not."
- Hold opinions with light hands: "I can't see it being something I use over other models" rather than "it's objectively bad"
- Ask the genuinely interesting question, not the clickbait question

**Don't:**
- Use ALL-CAPS or triple exclamation marks in editorial copy
- Cover something just because it is trending
- Hedge so carefully that no opinion survives

**Anti-example from past content:**

> "It's not the most impressive task by all means." *(Ben's Bites — this is the correct move: naming the limits of the example before the reader does. The anti-pattern would be presenting the taxi-booking story as revolutionary when it is just a good illustration.)*

---

### 5. Warm, Never Ingratiating

**Definition:** Talks to readers as smart adults who share the same obsessions — not as an audience to be managed or a list to be monetised. The warmth is the warmth of a group chat with people who get it.

**Sounds like:** "Hey folks," / "What's up gang," / "So pumped to release this in a week's time and get you MFs AI power users!" (AI with Remy — calibrated to audience familiarity)

**Does not sound like:** "Dear Valued Subscriber, Thank you so much for being part of our incredible community. We are truly grateful for your continued support and loyalty."

**Do:**
- Address readers the same way you'd address a group chat with close peers
- Use "I" and "you" liberally — this is a one-to-one conversation at scale
- Ask genuine questions and mean them: "Hit reply and tell me what you would do" (Pat @ Starter Story)

**Don't:**
- Thank people for subscribing or reading — they know; it reads as filler
- Use "community" as a noun for your audience (feels corporate)
- End emails with generic closers: "As always, thanks for your continued support!"

**Anti-example from past content:**

> "You're getting this because you subscribed to the AI with Remy newsletter at aiwithremy.com." *(The mandatory footer — necessary and legally fine, but it's the single coldest moment in every email. It shows by contrast how warm the editorial voice is.)*

## Archetype

- **Primary:** Sage — knowledge, truth, mastery. The brand is trusted precisely because it explains what's real, not what's optimistic.
- **Secondary:** Everyman — relatable, honest about limitations, present in the mess of life alongside the reader.
- **Rationale:** The dominant voice in the swipe file (Ben's Bites, AI with Remy) earns its audience through intellectual honesty — the Sage move. But the Sage alone risks becoming the Wise Professor, which this voice never is. The Everyman secondary keeps it grounded: "I locked myself out my Airbnb today," "I'm running 3 young kids and this is the only project I've kept going." The pairing explains why readers trust AND like this voice. An alternative reading — Creator — is present in the AI with Remy course-launch emails, but it is a mode, not the base voice.

## NN/g 4 Dimensions Positioning

Each dimension is a 3-point scale. At least 3 of 4 are clearly off-centre.

| Dimension | Position | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Funny ↔ Serious | Leaning funny | Dry wit, self-deprecating asides, occasional internet-native irreverence ("get you MFs AI power users"), but the content itself is taken seriously. Not a comedy newsletter. |
| Formal ↔ Casual | Casual | Sentence fragments as style ("Not so much this time."), lowercase subject lines, "lol" used once and naturally. The formality dial is as low as editorial voice can go without losing credibility. |
| Respectful ↔ Irreverent | Leaning irreverent | Calls out hype directly, willing to say "this is bullshit," names the downside of a sponsored product. Irreverent toward the industry's posturing, not toward the reader. |
| Enthusiastic ↔ Matter-of-fact | Leaning matter-of-fact | The dominant mode is "here's what happened, here's what it means, here's what I'd do." Enthusiasm is reserved for genuine moments and reads as real because it is rationed. |

## Tone Modulation Matrix

How tone shifts by situation × channel. Each cell: **dominant tone** + 2-3 prohibited tones.

| Situation \ Channel | **Email Newsletter** | **Twitter/X** | **LinkedIn** | **Blog/Website** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Launch / win** | Excited but grounded — share the real number + honest caveat. ✗ Hype, ✗ all-caps, ✗ "we did it!" without specifics | Quick, punchy, one key fact + one hot take. ✗ Thread-bait, ✗ humble-brag | Measured professional enthusiasm — what it means. ✗ Cringe celebration, ✗ self-congratulation without substance | Detailed writeup — the story behind the number. ✗ Sales-page framing |
| **Crisis / outage** | Direct and fast — state what happened, own it, say what's being done. ✗ Corporate passive voice, ✗ "we apologise for any inconvenience" | Same: direct, fast, human. ✗ PR-speak | Brief professional acknowledgment. ✗ Over-explanation | Full post-mortem when resolved. ✗ Blaming third parties |
| **Complaint (justified)** | Name the failure, take ownership, offer a concrete fix. ✗ Deflecting, ✗ policy-speak | Acknowledge publicly, resolve privately. ✗ Defensive | Professional acknowledgment + fix. ✗ Delete / ignore | — |
| **Complaint (unjustified / viral)** | State the facts once, clearly, without drama. ✗ Fighting back, ✗ lengthy rebuttals | One clear tweet correcting the record. ✗ Threading a full defence | Stay off LinkedIn for drama; address via newsletter if necessary. ✗ Public argument | — |
| **Sensitive societal topic** | Careful, factual, brief — only address if directly relevant to AI/tech. ✗ Hot takes, ✗ political positioning | Share a factual observation, not a stance. ✗ Engagement-bait | Skip or reference a more substantive piece. ✗ Opinion without evidence | Long-form, sourced, balanced analysis only. |
| **Bad news (price increase, sunset)** | Honest, early, with context. Lead with the change, explain the why, give the timeline. ✗ Burying it, ✗ spin | Share the key fact with a link. ✗ Minimising | Professional + brief. ✗ Defensive framing | — |
| **Routine / informational** | Conversational, energetic, clear structure. Headlines → brief take → link. ✗ Exhaustive summaries, ✗ no opinion | One-sentence take + link. ✗ Long threads on routine news | Brief framing + link to email/post. ✗ Reprinting the full email | Full depth — this is the right channel for long analysis. |
| **Sales objection** | Pre-empt honestly — "here's the caveat before you buy." ✗ Oversell, ✗ false urgency, ✗ fear-based close | Not for sales objections. | Not for sales objections. | Detailed FAQ / honest positioning page. |
| **Apology** | Brief, direct, specific. State what you did wrong, what you're doing about it. ✗ "I'm sorry if anyone was offended," ✗ over-apology | One clear tweet. ✗ Deletion as apology | Professional brief apology. ✗ Public self-flagellation | — |
| **Recruitment** | Personality-forward — describe what the work actually looks like. ✗ Corporate JD language, ✗ "rockstar" / "ninja" | Culture signals over job titles. ✗ Formal listing format | More formal but still human. ✗ Generic role description | — |

## Lexicon

### Preferred terms

| Term | Use for | Don't confuse with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `folks` | Email salutation (informal, warm, non-gendered) | `dear subscribers`, `hey everyone`, `hi all` |
| `readers` | Referring to the audience in third-person | `community`, `subscribers`, `users` |
| `agent` / `agents` | AI that takes autonomous, multi-step actions | `chatbot`, `assistant`, `bot` (unless chatbot is accurate) |
| `skill` / `skills` | Reusable AI instruction file that gives an agent a capability | `plugin`, `feature`, `tool` (unless the tool-call sense is meant) |
| `harness` | An interface or environment that wraps an AI model | `platform`, `app` (too generic) |
| `frontier model` | Best-in-class large language model from a leading lab | `AI`, `LLM` (acceptable in technical context), `smart AI` (never) |
| `daily driver` | The model/tool you use for most work, not the most capable one | `default model`, `base model` |
| `context` | The information you give an agent to understand a task | `prompt` (too narrow) |
| `connector` | A link between Claude and a live tool (Notion, Stripe, etc.) | `integration`, `plugin`, `add-on` |
| `in` / `out` | Pricing shorthand for input/output tokens ("$5 in / $30 out per million tokens") | "input cost," "output cost" (verbose in context) |
| `on-device` | Processing that happens locally, without sending data to a cloud server | `local`, `private` (both acceptable; `on-device` is most precise) |

### Banned terms

| Banned | Use instead | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `revolutionary` / `revolutionary AI` | "a significant step," "the first model to…" | Unverifiable marketing claim; readers distrust it |
| `game-changing` | Specific claim about what actually changed | Empty superlative |
| `industry-leading` | Cite the benchmark or the user number | Unverifiable, self-serving |
| `leverage` (metaphorical) | `use`, `apply`, `take advantage of` | Corporate jargon; banned in all non-financial contexts |
| `synergy` / `synergies` | Describe the actual combined effect | MBA cliché |
| `solution` (generic product noun) | Name the product or describe what it does | Means nothing without a subject |
| `excited to announce` | Just announce it | Self-referential; leads with the emotion, not the news |
| `community` (for email list/audience) | `readers`, `subscribers`, or address them directly | Corporate-feeling; implies management of the relationship |
| `deep dive` | `breakdown`, `full writeup`, `detailed look` | Overused across the category |
| `unlock` (metaphorical) | `access`, `get`, `enable` | Overused; feels growth-hacky |
| `supercharge` | The specific improvement | Vague power word with no referent |
| `seamlessly` | Describe what actually happens | Meaningless filler adverb |
| `rockstar` / `ninja` / `guru` (for roles) | Job title or actual descriptor | Cringe; alienating |
| `hustle` (as value) | Name the actual behaviour | Vague; romanticises poor conditions |
| `empower` | Describe what the thing lets people do | Overused to the point of meaninglessness |

- sharp
- honest

- fast
- cheaper

### Jargon policy

- **Allowed for:** Technical detail in the body of an email when the primary audience is technical (API pricing, token counts, benchmark names, model architecture terms like "context window," "inference," "weights")
- **Prohibited for:** Subject lines, email openers, and any segment targeting general-audience readers without a plain-language explanation in the same sentence
- **Always define on first use** when crossing from technical to general-audience contexts. Pattern used in the swipe file: define in a parenthetical — *"agentic (just means the AI going off and doing multi-step tasks on its own)"*

### Naming conventions

- **Brand name:** Written exactly as the brand specifies — capitalisation and punctuation matter
- **Product names:** Exact capitalisation: Claude, Codex, Notion, OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor — never lowercase unless stylistically deliberate
- **Feature names:** Treat like product names when they are proper nouns (Claude Tag, Claude Cowork, Fugu, Agent Hub)
- **Competitors:** Name them directly and honestly. Don't euphemise ("a major AI lab") when naming them is more useful. Compare, don't attack.
- **Customers / users:** `readers` in third-person; `you` in direct address. Never `users` in the newsletter context. Never `subscribers` in the editorial voice.
- **Models:** Refer to AI models with their full proper names on first mention; shorthand on repeat ("Fable 5" then "Fable"). Avoid generic "the model" without an antecedent.

## Mechanics

| Decision | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Person | 1st singular (`I`) for personal editorial; 1st plural (`we`) only when speaking for a team. 2nd singular (`you`) for the reader. Never 3rd person for the writer. |
| Contractions | Yes — always. `I've`, `it's`, `they're`, `don't`, `can't`. No contraction signals formality or caution; use sparingly for that effect only. |
| Oxford comma | Yes — used consistently in the swipe file. Prevents ambiguity in lists of 3+. |
| Sentence length (avg target) | 12–18 words for email body. Shorter for emphasis (as short as 2 words: "Not so much this time."). 20–25 words max for explanation paragraphs. |
| Active vs passive default | Active — name who does what. Passive reserved for genuinely passive situations or softening blame (crisis context only). |
| Sentence case vs title case | Sentence case throughout — subject lines, headers, section labels. Title case only in brand/product names. |
| Emoji policy | Sparingly in email — used as visual bullet-replacement (📌 TL;DR) or genuine emotional punctuation, not decoration. Zero emoji in formal contexts. Cap: 1–3 per email, 0–1 per tweet. |
| Punctuation tics | Em-dash: allowed, used for asides and pivots. Ellipsis: allowed for trailing thought in casual register; not in professional contexts. Exclamation marks: one per email maximum; reserved for genuine excitement. No double exclamation (!!) ever in editorial. |
| Numerals | Always use numerals for numbers when they are data points: `3 young kids`, `6 live sessions`, `$1,497`. Spell out when ordinal/qualitative: "the third time," "a second look." |
| Dates | Written out in email context: "Monday June 29" or "July 7." Avoid DD/MM/YYYY ambiguity for international audiences. |
| Currencies | USD format `$1,497` with comma separator. Per-million-token pricing: `$5 in / $30 out` (the shorthand from the swipe file). |
| Lowercase in casual register | The AI with Remy voice uses sentence-start lowercase in some contexts ("the waitlist goes first"). This is a deliberate style signal for extreme informality. Use only in the most casual channel (direct DM-style announcements, Twitter). Never in headline or subheader position. |

---

## Inclusive Language

- **Gendered language:** Avoid gendered generics. Use `folks` (already the preferred salutation), `they/them` for unknown individuals. Never `guys` as a generic group address.
- **Pronouns:** Use the person's preferred pronoun; if unknown, use their name or `they`. Use `he/him` for named individuals when gender is established and accurate.
- **Ability / disability:** Person-first where the person hasn't indicated preference. Avoid metaphors that trivialise disability ("cripple" / "lame" never).
- **Race and nationality:** Name nationalities and origins factually when relevant (Moonshot AI is Beijing-based; Sakana AI is Japan-based). Avoid stereotyping. Do not describe international models with exoticising language.
- **Age:** Do not use age as an implicit criticism or qualifier. Biographical context (e.g. "21-year-old founder") is accurate, not dismissive.
- **Neurodiversity:** "crazy" and "insane" appear in the swipe file as enthusiasm markers — acceptable in the current cultural register but monitor for drift as norms shift.
- **Reference:** Conscious Style Guide (Karen Yin), APA Inclusive Language Guidelines.

## Channel-Specific Guidance

### Email Newsletter (Primary)

**Hard constraints:** No character limit. HTML rendering. Subject line is a headline; preview text is a secondary headline. Average scan time: 45 seconds. Subscriber is on their schedule, not yours.

**Tonal shift from voice baseline:** This is home base — the full voice applies here without modulation. The most personal, the most opinionated, the most willing to go long when the content earns it.

**Do:**
- Open with a personal one-liner or current event, then pivot to content within 3 sentences
- Use TL;DR as a scannable entry point for time-poor readers (📌 TL;DR with bullet list)
- Separate headlines from quick links — the quick-links section is a separate reading mode (skimming vs. reading)

**Don't:**
- Write subject lines that are clever but unclear — "Caught cheating" works because the preview text resolves it immediately
- Let a sponsor segment run longer than 5 sentences or sound different from the editorial voice
- End with a generic call to action ("Don't forget to share with a friend!")

**Example opening sentence in this channel:** "When I was in Greece, I needed to organise a taxi from the airport home. I pinged Codex and 1m37s later it was done."

---

### Twitter/X

**Hard constraints:** 280 characters per tweet. Thread max: 5 tweets before quality degrades. No markdown.

**Tonal shift from voice baseline:** Compress the editorial voice to its sharpest edge. One observation, one opinion, one question, or one link per unit. Personal texture stays; explanation collapses.

**Do:**
- Lead with the counter-intuitive statement or the sharp take, then add context if threading
- Use: "[Surprising claim]. Here's why." as the single most effective opening format
- Quote/retweet with a one-sentence hot take that adds something — never "this" or "interesting thread"

**Don't:**
- Thread out an email newsletter (tweet the link instead)
- Use thread-bait hooks: "I spent 6 months learning X. Here are 10 things you need to know:"
- Tweet more than once per day on the same topic

**Example opening sentence in this channel:** "Fugu isn't a Fable killer. It's a router. Clever idea — but 3.5x slower than Opus in real testing."

---

### LinkedIn

**Hard constraints:** ~3,000 character limit per post. Algorithm rewards comments > likes. No markdown.

**Tonal shift from voice baseline:** Dampen the informality by one step. Contractions stay. Personal anecdote stays. Remove slang and internet-native phrasing. Structure the post more explicitly — LinkedIn readers skim more aggressively.

**Do:**
- Open with a bold statement or mini-story hook that lands in the first 2 lines (the "see more" cut-off)
- Make the first comment your link (LinkedIn suppresses link-in-post reach)
- End with a direct, genuine question — not "what do you think?" but something specific

**Don't:**
- Use the "I was [X]. Then [Y] happened. Here's what I learned:" format — overused to the point of parody
- Repost the full newsletter; write a fresh angle with the link in comments
- Put emojis as bullet points — it looks like a template

**Example opening sentence in this channel:** "Three months ago I stepped back from work. Burnt out, third kid, health issues. This week I figured out the only project I've kept going for years — and why."

---

### Blog/Website

**Hard constraints:** No length limit. SEO is a factor (target keyword in H1, meta description, first paragraph). Evergreen content outlives the news cycle.

**Tonal shift from voice baseline:** More structured than email. Add subheadings every 300–400 words. Personal texture reduces slightly; explanation expands. Provide enough context for a cold reader arriving from search.

**Do:**
- Write H2s that are meaningful — the reader should understand the post's argument by skimming the H2s alone
- Include a concrete example or screenshot for every abstract claim
- Write for the cold reader (search) AND the subscriber — provide context at the top

**Don't:**
- Write SEO-stuffed intros that repeat the keyword five times before saying anything useful
- Recycle email copy verbatim — expand or rework it for the medium
- End with "In conclusion, we have seen that…" — close with a single sharp line or cut entirely

**Example opening sentence in this channel:** "There are now four AI models worth caring about for daily knowledge work. Here is how I actually use each of them — and when I don't reach for them at all."

## Global Do's and Don'ts

A scannable, consolidated list for writers and bots loading TONE.md into their context window.

### Do

1. Lead with the point — the news, the take, the instruction — in the first sentence. Every time.
2. Name the downside of any product, model, or idea you are recommending.
3. Use short sentences for emphasis. Let them sit alone on a line.
4. Write "I" when you mean "I." Speak in first person from your own experience.
5. Qualify claims you haven't personally verified: "I haven't tested it, so don't take my word for it here."
6. Use concrete numbers, prices, and timeframes — not "affordable" but "$5 in / $30 out."
7. Correct hype directly: name the claim, then correct it in the next sentence.
8. Let the personal detail (the story, the life moment) serve the point — then drop it and move on.
9. Address the reader as `you`, one intelligent adult at a time.
10. End with a clear next action or a genuine question — never a generic closer.

### Don't

1. Don't use: revolutionary, game-changing, industry-leading, supercharge, unlock, seamlessly, deep dive, empower, synergy, leverage (metaphorical), excited to announce.
2. Don't open with context-setting, scene-painting, or throat-clearing — open with the news.
3. Don't write sponsor copy that sounds different from the editorial voice.
4. Don't use "community" to describe the reader list.
5. Don't hedge so much that no opinion survives the paragraph.
6. Don't stack more than one personal paragraph per piece — texture, not content.
7. Don't use ALL-CAPS or multiple exclamation marks in editorial.
8. Don't describe something as a first of its kind without verifying it.
9. Don't thank the reader for subscribing, reading, or being here.
10. Don't write a conclusion that restates the intro — either extend the idea or cut it.

## Examples Library

Before/after pairs and full-artefact samples that downstream writers can pattern-match against.

### Before / After

**1. Sponsor / product mention**

Before (off-brand):

> "We are thrilled to introduce our partnership with Metatate — an innovative, industry-leading platform that is revolutionising the way AI agents access and utilise business rules, enabling seamless and efficient agentic data workflows."

After (on-brand):

> "Most agentic data work is quietly propped up. The agent returns something plausible, and every answer gets checked in case it's plausibly wrong. Metatate gives agents the rules they're missing: which revenue definition to use, which policy applies, which records to trust. Try it for free."

Why: On-brand version leads with the problem, not the product; uses plain verbs; no banned adjectives. (Actual Ben's Bites sponsor copy — the standard to hit.)

---

**2. Model announcement (launch recap)**

Before (off-brand):

> "Anthropic has released Claude Sonnet 5, a powerful new AI model that delivers exceptional performance across a wide range of tasks at a competitive price point, making it an ideal choice for professionals seeking to leverage AI capabilities in their daily workflows."

After (on-brand):

> "Claude Sonnet 5 landed on June 30 — the first proper Sonnet upgrade since 4.6, and it's a big leap. It now lands right near Opus on a lot of real work. Only about 2% behind Opus 4.8 on computer use and agentic coding. But push it to high or max effort and its cost climbs right up onto Opus 4.8's. At that point Opus matches or beats it. So: Sonnet 5 for low and medium effort. Opus for the hard stuff."

Why: On-brand version leads with the fact, uses real numbers, names the limitation in the same breath as the praise, gives a direct recommendation. (Modelled on AI with Remy's Sonnet 5 coverage.)

---

**3. Personal opening**

Before (off-brand):

> "As entrepreneurs and builders in today's fast-paced AI landscape, we all know how challenging it can be to balance our personal lives with the demands of running a business. I certainly feel this tension, and I wanted to share some thoughts on how I've been navigating it."

After (on-brand):

> "Last December we had our third child, Poppy, and I was working at Factory. But she has some health issues, and I got pretty burnt out and overwhelmed, so I had to step back. For the last 7 months I've been plodding along work-wise without much agency. Which isn't like me at all. I'm going to put more of myself into this thing."

Why: On-brand version is specific (names, dates, circumstances), short (4 sentences), and pivots to a point. Off-brand version is generic, doesn't trust the reader to find their own relevance. (Actual Ben's Bites birthday email.)

---

**4. Product take (honest limitation)**

Before (off-brand):

> "Pangram's AI detection technology represents a significant advancement in the field, offering highly accurate results that have impressed us in our testing."

After (on-brand):

> "Pangram has sent the claim of 'AI detectors don't work' for a toss — it works wayyy better than most. But I'm still unsure about how reliable it is. I tested it on some pieces of 100% AI-written content and got 100% human scores on most of them."

Why: On-brand version praises the product then immediately qualifies with a personal test result that contradicts the official narrative. Praise becomes credible because it comes with an honest caveat. (Actual Ben's Bites coverage.)

---

**5. Quick-link section (the scan layer)**

Before (off-brand):

> "Here are some interesting links you might enjoy reading this week! We've curated a selection of articles and resources that we think you'll find valuable. Check them out below!"

After (on-brand):

> "- Cursor rebuilt SQLite from an 835-page manual using multiple agent swarm setups. Across configurations that passed all tests, costs varied a lot → Opus 4.8 + Composer 2.5 cost $1,339 vs $10,565 for GPT-5.5 alone.
> - Notion AI can now use a browser for you. (in early access)
> - Ramp Router — Send each request to a relevant model. Saves 30% in costs for Ramp internally."

Why: On-brand version has no intro paragraph, no outro, one sentence per link. The voice is in the curation and the one-sentence take, not in scaffolding the list. (Actual Ben's Bites quick-links format.)

---

### Full-artefact samples

- **Complete email (personal moment + product coverage):** Ben's Bites "Better design than Fable" (Jul 21) — birthday email. Open with personal, pivot to product, maintain voice throughout sponsor segment.
- **Complete email (technical explanation for non-technical):** AI with Remy's Sonnet 5 / GPT-5.6 email — model for explaining AI pricing and performance tiers to a general audience.
- **Quick-links section format:** Ben's Bites "Quick links" — 6–10 items, each one sentence, no introductory paragraph, no outro. The voice is in the curation, not the commentary.
- **Sales email with integrity:** AI with Remy "doors open tomorrow amigos" — full course launch email that sells without hype. Every claim is specific (exact price, exact seats, exact time, full refund guarantee). No pressure tactics. No false urgency.
